summary: The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 representing accrued interest on the amount borrowed by the assessee from its customers. The Wealth Tax officer included a sums of Rs, 1,00,000 estimated as the accrued interest. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the accrued Interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessment of the assessee. The High Court dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date. It includes the assets which are not confined to cash. [309 D] (2) The Wealth tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the deceased if he were alive. [310 E] (3) The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the assesses. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be excluded within the assets. [311 G H] Commissioner of Wealth tax vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju, (Orissa) (4) The assets are not restricted to cash and it is apparent from the definition or "net Wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value". of all the debts owed by the assesee on the valued date. [313 F] Commissioner Of Wealth Tax vs V.ysy Kumar Basu, ; , referred to. (5) The asset is not confined only cash. It would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. It was apparent that What accrues as an right also fell to be include within the wealth Tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assesees are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lending business are liable to included in net wealth. [334 C D] Commissioner for Wealth tax, West Bengal vs Vithysy Rao Badrealarayana Moorten Kumar Basu vs Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bihar & Orissa, ; and Commissioner of wealth tax vsVysyayaraju Bcadreenarayana MOorthy Raju (Orissa), (supra) and by the Karnataka High Court in A. T. In the instant case, the assets are neither confined to a cash nor hybecrid.

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was recognised by the Cashier since he kn ew him personally. The Inquiry Officer found all the three guilty of the charge framed against each of them. The respondent moved the High Court under Article 226 challenging the findings of inquiry offi cer as well as the order of dismissal passed by the compe tent authority. The Tribunal held that the applicant was not a "Lastly" employee and therefore, he was not entitled to any relief in respect of charges l(a) and l(d) of the Punjab Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1965. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even if there were amongst the reasons given by the Commissione r, some which were extraneous, if the rest were relevant a nd could be considered sufficient, the Commissioner 's conclu sions would not be vitiated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that even though there were among the reasons stated by the Commissioner, some what were extraneous and if the remaining two were relevant, a nd can be considered adequate having regard to t he misdemeanour established. [529G] 1.2 In dismissing the appeal of the respondent, this Court set aside t he impugned order of penalty on the ground that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon him was whi ch was disproportionate to the gravi ty of the charges proved against him and is in stark contrast to the punishment awarded to his other three colleagues in whose cases, only future increments were stopped. [629G H] 1:3 The High court was right In holding that t he penalty of dismiss ment from service inflicted upon the appellant was whol m been held to be disproportionate to gravi sion of the Charge proved against the respondent and is accordingly set aside with liberty to hold fresh enquiry. [613B C] 1 :4. The High ci lutions were not justified in interfering with the order passed by t he Tribunal in awarding the lesser punishment. [729G, 730A] 2.1 In view of the fact that the respondent was not working in his Division and had access to the records which 24 were fabricated at the relevant time, the Inquiry Officer had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty on him. The order of the High court is set aside. [625B C; 615C D] 3.2 The Tribunal has no jursidiction to interfere with the findings in respect o f charges l (a) & l(e) and charge 2 need not be disturbed. [700D E] 4.3 In view Of the fact, that the appellant had access t to the record which 24 was fabricated at a relevant time the Inquiry Commis sioner found all th three guilty guilty of charge framed by him against each one of them, it is necessary to modify the punishment award to the applicant. [600D] 4:4 The High Ci l Court has no jurisdiction in interfering wit h the order dated 5th May, 1985 passed by it in exercise of its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution.

The plaintiff, who was the lawful tenant of the property, filed a suit for an injunction restraining the defendants from dispossessing him from the property in dispute. The Trial Court decreed the suit on September 25, 1985. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the suit was barred by res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 1 and hence the latter was in lawful possession of the said property and since he had not been dispossessed,in accordance with law the decree for eviction could not lie. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed in the subsequent suit that the subsequent suits would be barred by limitation. [1023B] In the instant case, what procedure should the Civil Court follow in such situations? The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section 58(2) of the Act. [ 1024C D] In view of this clear provision of Order 2 Rule 2 CPC it is not necessary to decide whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant under the Act, but that procedure should be followed in such situation. [925D E] The suit was dismissed on technical ground that the plaintiff had paid a sum of Rs. 1 in collusion with defendant No.2 and hence irrespective of the reliefs claimed in subsequent suit, the second one was clearly barred by principle of res judicata.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. They also seek regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The case of the Corporation is that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The petitioners are employed as daily rated employees and they demand payment for equal work at that of other drivers. It was also stated that the petitioners are supplied with the necessary tools for carry ing out their work and also working uniforms like aprons and overalls. A little more information about the purpose and object of the corporation would be useful for proper understanding of the case. The Corporation has suffered huge loss and the total losses accumulated hitherto is Rs.69.77 lakhs. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that there was bumper cases filed in this Court for enforcement of the right to equal pay for equal Work. It is also contended that the principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. The Court pointed out that the principles of " equal pay" have no mechanical Application in every cases of similar nature. The principle of 'equal pay ' has no independent application in each case of identical work. It cannot be evaluated by the mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. So long as such value judgment is made bona fide, reasonably on an intelligible criterion which has a rational nexus with the object of dif ferentiation, such differentiation will not amount to discrimination. The doctrine of equal pay cannot be enforced. It can be evaluated either by the bare volume of works, there might be qualitative differences as regards quality and responsibility; there may also be qualitative distinction as regards authenticity and responsibility but the duties make a distinction. So far as skilled and unskilled workers in class IV employees in Government service are concerned, they execute the work in their own homes. It has suffered considerable loss and it is thus a service oriented organisation helping the village artisans and craftsmen to produce and market their products on remunerative prices. The State has suffered heavy losses and thetotal losses accumulated thereafter is Rs,69.76 lakhs. Hence, the petition fails and is dismissed. P.S.

The prosecution case was that on 14.11.1972 at about 4.15 p.m. the accused persons were armed with deadly weapons and they assaulted Malan and his wife, PW 1, who was a student of B.B.B., in the school. The deceased was aged 40 years and was residing with her parents. On the date of occurrence he was aged 12 years. He was aged about 12 years at the time of incident. He had been living with his parents. His father was aged 38 years at that time. He died on 2.1.1976. The accused persons pleaded innocence and claimed to be tried along with them for the murder of Malan, and for the death of Malin. The Sessions Judge acquitted all the seven accused but convicted them under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 304 Part II I. P.C., and also to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000 each. In appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 and 6. The State filed Criminal Appeal 38 of 1977 for enhancement of the sentence of imprisonment for death of the deceased. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: (1) It is well settled that in a case where two or more persons are required for an offence of conspiracy under section 120A I.PC., they cannot be convicted for the same offence unless there is some evidence to show that the accused had conspired with the seven other accused to commit the murder. [623D] (2) The prosecution has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that accused 6 was found in the company of accused 7 and the approver P.W. 1 against accused 6 as reliable and the judicial confession, Exh. 31), was recovered from the house of accused 6. There is no evidence to establish beyond reasonable doubts that accused 2 was found at the place where the murder took place. [643E] (3) The mere fact that the deceased was a child does not make any difference in the case of the prosecution. [641G] (4) The circumstances and the finding of the High court that the approver ' P.Ws. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 were found in possession of accused 8 and the evidence of the approver is corroborated by the medical evidence.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, filed a suit for declaration that the gift deed was void and that she had no right to create liability in any way in favour of her husband Sadagopalachar. The trial court held that the will was not proved to be the last will of the testator but it further held that there was sufficient evidence to prove the execution of the will. In appeal, the High Court agreed with the finding of the trial court and dismissed the suit. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The onus of proving a will is on the propounder who alleges the exercise of undue influence, fraud or coercion in respect of the execution thereof. [4A B] (2) The burden of proving that a will set up by the propounder is proved to have been executed was not discharged by the court below. It is true she A as an old woman of 64 years and had been ailing for some time before the will, but even without such pleas circumstances may raise a doubt as to whether the testator was acting of his own free will in executing the will propounded, such pleas may have to be proved by the caveators; but, even without these pleas circumstances might raise a suspicion as to how it is to be established. [441 D] (3) The propounder must prove that the testator had acted of his free will and he knew the Junior Kulbagal who was working as a Cane Superintendent in the said factory. It would be a part of the initial onus to remove any such legitimate doubts in the matter. [442 E F] Bai Gungabai vs Bhugwandas Valji, ; , referred to. (4) The will must be read out by the testatrix and it adds that the testatrix had not executed any prior will but that in case any such will has been executed by her the same stood cancelled by the execution. [443 D] Bai Mongabai vs Gungbai, A.I.R.

The appellant company, a manufacturer of Arc Carbons, manufactured by the appellant company. The appellant company had not produced their account books to show that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. The Sales Tax authorities rejected the claim of the appellant on the ground that they fall under entry No. 18 of the Madras Act and held that they fell within entry No, 18 of Schedule 1 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the use which is generally made of the arc carbons under consideration links the taxable object with its general or ordinary use, was not a "agricultural machinery" within the meaning of entry 18 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. HELD: (1) The word "electrical valves" used in Entry No. 3 of Schedule I of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1953, is not confined to particular machines for which they; may serve as aids. [890 B] (2) The entry No., 18 of schedule 1 of an entirely different Act of a different State, is clearly intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof" in the Madras Sales Tax, Act, 1957, as modified subsequently, which read: "bicycles, tricycles and cycle rickshaws and perambulators and parts and accessaries thereof other than tyres and tubes". [891 C] (3) The words "electric valves" are not necessarily confined to specific machines for the purpose of making them. [889 D E] (4) The use of the word "cinema" in Entry 18 of Part II of Schedule II of Mysore Sales tax Act, 1959, is a device which assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the levy was arbitrary and violative of Article 301 of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposed a restriction on movement of goods from one State to another for the purpose of mining does not involve any movement as such. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The levy is arbitrary and discriminatory. It is well settled that a classification to be valid has to satisfy two conditions: (i) that there is an intelligible differentia between those who are included in the class which is affected by any law or rule and those who were placed outside the said rule; and (ii) that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there was no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution. [410C D] 1.2 The levy being arbitrary, it is not open to challenge on the ground that it imposed unreasonable restrictions on movement from one state to another. [416B C] 1:3 In the instant case the levy is made under a law made by the Central Gov ernment. It was increased to Rs.7. per metric tonne which had been fixed in 1981 and in 1985 it was increased upto Rs. 7. per cubic metre which had already been fixed at Rs. 3.50 per cubic metres. The levy was therefore, being levied under a statute made by Parliament to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was made applicable to the whole of India. [413D E] 1 :4.1 In view of the fact that the petitioners had been granted mining lease in respect of minor minerals, they were not entitled to any royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the royalty payable by them. [414E F] 2.2 There is no reason why the levy should be enhanced on the minor minerals which had not been fixed under a contract entered into with the State Government or the Central Government. The imposition being arbitrary and unreasonable, it was not open for the petitioners to challenge the validity thereof on the grounds that (i ) there was an intelligible nexus between those whose annual production was not exceeding two lakhs bricks per year and who were placing outside the aforesaid rule; (ii ) there is no reasonable connection between the Classification for purposes o the proviso under rule 1 to rule 20 to show concessions in the matters of payment, of royalty, the social Policy underlying the constitution, the statute and the Rules. [411D E]. 3. The impost being arbitrary it was open to the petitioners not to challenge it on the plea that there had been an intelligible distinction between those whom are included within the class who were included in that class which was affected by a law or Rule and those whose persons take quarrying parawana, are persons of the weaker section of society. [409D E; 414E F]. 3:1 The imposition is arbitrary. It has to be based on some rational basis. [420B] 2:2 In the present case the impost was made under an Act made by a competent authority and it had been imposed in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Act. The Act has made provision with regard to the issue of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect o minor minerals other than minor minerals and the procedure to be followed in that connection in the context of the provisions contained in the Act, the Rules and the rules.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village. The Commissioner held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The Subordinate Judge held that he was a "exempted" temple under the provisions of Madras Act 1 of 1925. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was a mere trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951, and that the suit had been filed by him in his capacity as trustee for a period of one year each at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. Held: (i) The succession to the office of trustee in the present case was for a fixed period of time and not for life; (ii) the appellant must be held to be a hereditary tenant within the ambit of section 4(9), and that he must be deemed to have been a trustee within section 6 (9) Of Act 19 Of 1951. The question whether the respondent is a hereditary trustees within the definition of the word "succession" in section 2(9)(a) of Act 19of 1951, was not one of fact but of law and it could not be said to be hereditary. In the present appeal the appellant has failed to establish that he is a mere holder of an office of hereditary trustee within his meaning of the section. The respondent was not merely an anomaly, it was an impossible legal position. (iii) The question as to whether the appellant is a "subaession" within the expression "sucession" or not must depend upon the choice of any individual. But the election to the Office of trustee is for a specified period of two years and not during life. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely a anomaly, but the right of the latter should not depend upon independent title, I am inclined to the view that the office cannot be saidto be hereditary unless the ,founder has laid down a special scheme of succession or except when usage or custom to the contrary is proved to exist. In this case the custom in (1) (2) 63 I.A. 57. (4) 70 I. A. 448. (5) A.LR. 1954 S.C. 606. (6) A,LR. (7) A and B are hereditary trustees because their office devolves by hereditary right or because succession to that office is not specifically provided for by the founder himself who created the endowment. The fact of transmission of the rights, estate, obligations and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs does not rest upon independent titles, I do not agree with the view taken by the Subordinate judge.

The appellant was charged under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the accused on the ground that the evidence of PW 4 was not reliable, because he had given a "candidate" to him in court, and that the prosecution witnesses were not examined by the defence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. There is no reason why those persons who are alleged to have inflicted these injuries must be presumed to have been present at the place of occurrence. [717B] 2. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. It is only necessary that the court should be circumspect and closely scrutinise the evidence to come to an unhesitating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. [617C] 3. The mere fact that PW 4 had stated in the first information report that "my elder brother" (meaning the deceased) was being chased by PWs 1 and 2 does not mean that his version in the FIR stands contradicted by the testimony in court on a very material point. It may not be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place where PW 4 did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. [613B C] 4. The evidence of PWs 1 to 3 is consistent and reliable, and there can be no infirmity in convicting the accused. [625E F] 5. The testimony of PWs 4 and 3 is corroborated by the evidence in court. It was also conceivable that those persons, who arrived at the scene of occurrence a little earlier than PW 4, did not know the assailants whom might have had already escaped, but they were told by PW 4 that it happened because while PW 4 went near his elder brother about hundred persons were there and "none of them asked him as to how it had happened". The very circumstance that this witness could not be persuaded so far as he is concerned was that while PW4 had stated that "the deceased) had been chased by PW 1, the accused was not implicated.

The assessee, a firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling tea in Bombay, was assessed to income tax under section 24B of the Income Tax Act. The assessment so made were for the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. Against that order an appeal was taken to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and then to the Tribunal. The matter was not pursued further by the Revenue but sometime later proceedings were started by the Income tax officer under section 34 in respect of the same income in the hands of "Amarchand N. Amarchand N., Mangaldas and Hiralal, in respect for the work done after December 1, 1949, the realisations were to be divided amongst Mangaldas, Hiralal and Ramesh. For the five assessment years 1951 52 and 1952 53 the assessee claimed that the realizations were to he divided among Mangaldas. The Appellate Assistant commissioner held that the notice under section34 could validly be served only for the assessments year 1950 51 and notices for subsequent years were invalid. Against this order an application was taken before the Incometax Officer under section 33B of Income tax Act, 1922, for the issue of a certificate to the assessee. The Tribunal held that on a correct interpretation of section 24 B the amounts which were received by the heirs and legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by them prior to the discontinuance of their practice but the Income ' tax Officer was not entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person. The High Court held that since the realisable payments were made subsequent to the previous year in which Amarchand died, the assessee could not be deemed to be an assessee for the purpose of assessment under section 23B as his income in his hands had been received before his death or by his heirs and Legal representatives after their death. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the fiction created by section 24A(1) of the Act is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received during his lifetime, income received subsequent to his death and fill up the lacuna which was pointed out by the High Court in Ellis C. J., in re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani, ; , that on an correct interpretation Of section 24(B) of Income Tax, 1922 the amounts received by a person after his lifetime should be treated as income received after his deceased death and that it was capital receipt and not revenue receipt. HELD : (i) The fiction is limited only to the case provided in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of s.24B. [707 B] (ii) Where a person dies before the publication of the notice referred to in sub sec.(1) or before he is served with a notice under sub section(2) of section 22 or before him is served, his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall, on the serving of the notices under sub s. (2), comply therewith and the Income. tax Officer can make assessment on the total profits of the person as if such executor, ad ministration or other Legal representative were the assessee for that year. [077 C] (iii) The words "the heirs andlegal representatives of a deceased person are liable to pay income tax out of his estate" in section 24D of the Indian Income Tax Rules, 1922. The fiction does not extend further than what is provided in section24 B.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They were appointed either directly or by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence Act, 1957 for domiciles of Telengana region will be immediately relieved from service. The action was based upon section 3 of the Public Employment Act,1957 (44 of 1957) which was an Act of Parliament made in pursuance of cl. (3) of article 16 of the Constitution. The petitioners were not appointed either by promotion nor by transfer or by any other local authority within a State or Union territory prior to appointment. They filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the action on the ground that they were discriminated against as they had been appointed between January 19, 1969 and July 5, 1968 and that their case was that article 16(3) under which the Act and the Rules purport to be made has been misunderstood as conferring a power to make, a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the petitioners were discriminated on account of the fact that they had not been appointed either through promotion or transfer to vacancies reserved under section 3(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that article 14 of the constitution is not attracted because the Constitution does not concede supremacy, Parliament must act within its appointed functions and not transgress them. HELD : (i) The power to create residential qualification for employment is thus exclusively conferred on Parliament. [121 C] (ii) The word 'under any State specified in the First Schedule or any local or other authority within its territory any requirement as regards residence in that State orUnion territory prior thereto appointment, as a condition of employment in the State or UNION territory prior or subsequent to such appointment, is not confined to residence within a part thereof. [122 D] (iii) The words 'residence within the State ' have been substituted by the words "residence in any particular part of India" in section 5 of the Andhra Act. The word "reship within the meaning of article 14 means residence within the territory of India and includes residence within that State. [123 E F] (iv) The expression "resencies within a state or Union Territory prior to such employment or appointment" is not restricted to residence outside the State but also includes residence in any part thereof, and it does not mean residence within any part of the State. It is only when Parliament makes a law that Parliament must make a provision regarding residence in the particular part thereof that Parliament can make a law in a special case prescribing any requirement As to residence under the Government of India Act, 1935, the present words from 'under the Government ' to 'Union territory ' have not been substituted. [124 E F; 125 A B] (v) The contention that article 19(1)(f) is attracted because Parliament has no power to enact a law for the more effective implementation of the law made by Parliament is misconceived. It does not say that Parliament cannot make a legislation in respect of residence in an particular part or any part therein. [125 E F]. (vi) The argument that article 21(1), which deals with residence within State, provides that no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory or any Union territory after he has been appointed to such office by promotion, or by direct requirement as required by the rules made under section 5.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them, also for offences punishable under sections 467 and 471 of the IPC. The trial court acquitted him of all these charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, the prosecution had failed to establish that the five registered letters in question were stolen by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The High Court has not found that there were compelling reasons for setting aside the acquittal of the accused. [413G H] (2) It is well settled that where the provisions of sections 103 and 165, Code of Criminal Procedure are contravened the search could be resisted by the person whose premises are sought to be searched. But to say that he must be deemed to be in exclusive possession of these articles and not merely in their joint possession along with his father because he had the opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he was in exclusive, possession would be arguing in a circle. [414B C] (3) The fact that they were found in the almirah which, at best, may be regarded as being in the joint possession of himself and his father would be argue in a Circle. [4) Section 55 of the Act runs thus : "Penalty for theft, dishonest misappropriation, secretion, destruction or throwing away of postal articles. Provided that where any person is found in an almirah, the key of which was produced by him shall be deemed not to be In use of the article and then inference can be drawn against him that he has secreted them from the mere fact that these were found at the time when they were recovered. [416B C; 416A] (4) The expression "in course of transmission by post" has been defined in section 3(a) of the , as follows : .lm15 " a postal article shall be presumed to be, in course of Transmission by post from the time of its being delivered to a Post Office to the time oucrse of transmission. [420B C]. (5) The word "in" has not been defined anywhere in section 2(a). It is only when the provisions are contravened that the search can be resisted on the ground that it was in contravention of the provisions. But, to say, that he should be deemed as in exclusive Possession of these article and not mere in their own possession alongwith his father. [411D] (6) The words "in order to be punished for secreting, destroying or throwing off a postal articles" have been defined by section 3 (a) as follows: .lnm15 A postal article may be deemed 'to be in course 'of transmission by posts from the place of its delivery to the addressee or of its having been returned to the sender or otherwise disposed of under Chapter VII. But if, therefore, it was the intention of the legislature that for an officer of the post office to be proceeded against for secretting, destroy or throwing in a postal parcel by post, entrustment of that article to him was essential it would have used language similar to that used by it in section 55. [441B C D] (7) The mere fact of seizure and recovery of the articles from the almirah did not make any difference as regards the place where the articles were found.

The appellants were convicted under section 5(1) of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 and sentenced to simple imprisonment for two weeks. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the order of stay passed by the Nyaya Panchayat was not a judicial order and that the High Court had erred in relying on this fact in its judgment. HELD : (i) The order sheet does not contain the .date of the order; even a copy of the telegram was not attached to the application; and the application seems to have been made after the proceedings on that date. [118C D] (ii) It is not proved on the evidence that any such application was made before the Nyaya panchayat. The only material before them was the application dated December 25, 1963, which was not supported by any affidavit sworn to or a certified copy of order; and even a photocopy of the letter was not annexed to the original application. [119D E] (iii) It seems to us that it is not established on the record that any application was filed before the Magistrate. The application dated 12th December, 1963 was not accompanied by an affidavit duly sworn to in or a Certified copy of its order. [120E F] (iv) The application did not contain any date of the High court 's stay order or the fact that the application was not being entertained by the Adalat. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him.

The appellant was charged with murder of Sheo Sahai. He was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death, but the High Court dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entire report dictated by the appellant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High court, fully make out the prosecution case against the appellant. HELD: (i) The statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant 's murder was inadmissible as it was not in evidence. [208 E] (ii) There is no reliable evidence to show that the appellant had committed the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed murder. It may be mentioned that the fact that he had the sword which was stained with human blood, leads to such a supposition, even if the mere possession of a sword so stained be not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder had committed an offence. [209 G H] (iii) The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive, to his extra judicial confessions, and that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. [207 E F] (iv) The High Court was wrong in rejecting the evidence of Ujagar singh about the murder. The fact that the accused had a sword which he was watching against the neel gais trespassing and grazing the crop, leads only to such an supposition. It is always difficult to find reasons for a person 's acting in a certain manner. [210 E F G] (v) The extra judicial confessional confession made by the Appellant to a police officer and that of the accused was not admissible in evidence, as there is good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on.

The appellants were elected to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December, 1978. The election was held on December 31, 1978 and 44 persons were declared elected. Thereafter the calendar of events was published on November 25, 1978 notifying that the poll, if necessary would take place on December31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants herein presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court praying for quashing the electoral roll and the calendar thereof issued for the purpose of the said election. The High Court dismissed the petition holding (i) that respondent No. 2 on October 20, 1978 had not refused to receive any such claim and (ii) that no person preferred any claim or objection after October 19, 1978 before respondent No 1. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the electoral rolls and the declaration of results of the election. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections could be preferred within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule 46 of the rules pending disposal of the petition. The writ petition was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High, Court on January 20, 1979 holding (ii), that respondent no. 2 had not denied the claim and/or objection filed beyond the prescribed period and that no such claim or objections could he preferred within a period of 30 days. On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants: (i ) that the delay involved in filing the writ petition before the high court was such that it dissentients a person to relief under Article 227 is a matter within the discretion of the Court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court had rightly dismissed the writ application holding (a) that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notices issued under rule 4(2) of Rules notifying the date for inclusion of names in the electoral Roll; and (b) that since respondent No 2 did not refuse to receive his applications, he was entitled to file a writ Petition immediately after the publication of such notice questioning its legality. [418C] 1.2 The High Courts had rightly held that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were not entitled to raise any objection or objection before the Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purposes. [409D] 1:3 In view of the fact that the petitioners did not know immediately after publication of notice under rule4(1), it was open to all persons who were interested in preferring claims or objections to file them within 30days from the day of publication thereof questioning its validity. No satisfactory reason for the delay was set out in the petition; and no satisfactory reasons for the delayed was set forth in the writ petitions referred to omissions of certain names from the electoral Rolls. No such appeal was presented. [420F] 1 :4 The question whether in a given case the delay is such that the dissentientents a man to relief against under Article226 is a matters within the discretionary discretion of High Court which, as in the all matters, of discretion have to exercise discretion judiciously and reasonable having regard regard to surrounding circumstances, are a matter for the discretion hasto exercise it judicially and reasonably.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The respondent company had been carrying on its business in sugar and molasses. It had been doing so for a long time. The company was not able to carry on its activities. The Company was not allowed to do so. The State Government issued notifications under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (the Act). The appellant company challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution and that it infringed article 14. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant company that the impugned Act satisfies even this test of rational classification. HELD: (1) The object of the Act is to prevent any person or class of persons from being singled out as a special subject for discriminatory and hostile legislation. It has the power to pick out a case of a person similarly situate and hand it over to the special tribunal and leave the case of the other person in the same circumstances to be tried by the procedure laid down in the Criminal Procedure Code. [529 C D] (2) The words "discrimi natory" and "hostile" are found to be used by American Judges often simultaneously and almost as synonymous expres sions in connection with discussions on the equal protection clause. [630 E F] (3) The expression "disCriti natory power" is not defined in the Act but has been used in a wide sense so as to include within its ambit all kinds of legislation which do not rest on classification, and no question of reasonable classification could fairly arise in respect of such (1).

The appellant was appointed as a Radiologist in the Medical College on September 9, 1966. The appellant was however, not appointed as an Associate Professor. He filed a return reiterating the stand taken by the Government of India in the Health Ministry that the experience gained by the appellant as an Assistant Professor in the Irwin Hospital cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of determining his eligibility for appointment as Associate Professor or Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College. The Specialists ' Grade II were appointed to the posts of Assistant Professors and Associate Professors on a fixed pay scale of Rs. 2750/ and Rs. Category (3) General Duty Officers Grade I, Grade II with a pay scale Rs. 3050/ respectively. The post which was required to be filling by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the posts in the junior scale who have rendered not more than six year of service as an Additional Professor were also required to do. Dar, Dr. Bose and others were appointed as Assistant Professors on fixed pay of Rs, Rs. 2850/ with a salary of Rs., Rs. 300/ respectively and Rs, 3050/- respectively. In the meanwhile, the appellant was promoted as an assistant Professor by the University of Delhi. The Government of Punjab issued a notification dated June 8, 1967 making substantive appointments of 80 officers to the Specialists Grade II (now Specialist Grade I Rs. 1800 2250) vacancies in Category 'B ' of the supertime scale and Specialists grade respectively with effect from September 9 1966. The said notification was challenged by the respondent on the ground that the appellant had been substantively appointed as Associate Professors in the Department of Radiotherapy in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi since he had rendered less than 6 years of experience in the post held by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the post which fell vacant on account of his being an Associate professor was not a teaching job and therefore the appellant could not be appointed by direct appointment as Professor or radiology in the department of Radiological Surgery in the Central Health Service. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High Court had erred in holding that there was 50% direct recruitment for the post to which he belonged and that the said 50% of vacancies were to have been filled by promotion from amongst the Professors who had been appointed as such in the year 1967. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The appellant who is a Radiographer in the Maulana Oxford Medical College cannot be appointed to by direct Recruitment as Professor of Radiology under r. 8 (2) of the CHS Rules, 1963. [8B] 1.2 The post held on September 7, 1966 was not an equivalent post for the purposes of his service conditions in the super time scale. It is a post belonging to Specialists Category II which practice is in the public interest and is essential for the maintenance of efficiency. The posts which cannot be filled through the UPSC before the rules came into being amended w.e.f. September 9 1967 are different and the appellant who was working as a doctor is allowed to compete with teachers in the teaching cadre, such teachers are at a disadvantage. [9C D] 1:3 It is not correct to say that these officers are recognised as teachers for the objects of their service conditions.

The Company was referred by the State Government under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that it would not be proper to compare the wage structure for these Paper Mills with that of the Company. On appeal by the Company, the High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the Tribunal to work out the minimum wages which should be paid on an entirely different basis. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The principle of industry cum region has to be applied by an Industrial Court when it proceeds to consider questions like wage structure, dearness allowance and similar conditions of service. [690 C] (2) The Tribunal committed a error in arriving at the decision and, consequently, the total minimum wage fixed by the High court must also be deemed to have the same break up. [667 D] (3) The question whether the Tribunal committed any error of law requiring interference by this Court is not one which could be considered as an issue for determination by the Industrial Tribunal. It is only in those cases that the Tribunal has worked out the surplus available on the correct basis, that surplus would have certainly justified grant of profit bonus at the rate of six months ' wages. [666 E] (4) The High Court committed a mistake in not taking into account the minimum wage which was fixed by it and in holding that there was no justification to introduce a new element of payment of bonus to casual and badIi workers at this stage.

The assessee, a company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961 to the assessee on the ground that the assessee had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that year, income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment for the relevant assessment years. The assessee challenged the validity of the notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notice on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Income Tax officer had no reasons to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of these assessee to disclose full and truly material facts, he was satisfied that it is a fit case for issue of a notice under s 148. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Income tax Officer has no power to issue a notice in respect of any assessment year. [446 B] (2) The report submitted by the Incometax Officer under section 151(2) does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it was a fit one for the issue of notice under Section 148. [449 C D] (3) The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to issue such a notice. He did not himself record that he was satisfaction that the income chargeable had escaped Assessment for that assessment year, and that there has been no omission or default as mentioned in section 147. [450 B] In the instant case, the Income. tax Officer did not itself record any reason why he could not have had reasons to suspect that by virtue of information in his possession, had reasons for believing that income chargeable under the Income 'tax Act had escaped assessments for that years. He was satisfied with the explanation and the report submitted under section151(2). [449 E] (4) The order passed by the Commissioner under section 147 is not a speaking one but a reasoned one. It does not say any reason to believe the reasons for coming before him. [451 C D].

The appellant firm was carrying on business in soap and umbrella businesses. The partnership deed provided that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income from the business was not discontinued because it had ceased to exist and its business was carried on thereafter by two independent firms. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) There is no warrant for the view for which the appellant contended that only the terms on which the business under the document of December 6, 1918 were carried on at the commencement of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, as claimed by the appellant, were revoked and not the head agreement to do business in partnership. [107 E] (2) The firm was dissolved so that it had been constituted by this document of October 30, 1943. It was not necessary for the purpose of section 25(1) to refer to the large number of cases in which the matter has been discussed, because the leading case on the subject of discontinuance is Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs P. It is hardly necessary to refer at once that there had been no succession and this case falls squarely within the rule of this Court in Figgies 's case. [108 E G] (3) The partnership was dissolved by a deed of dissolution signed by all the partners mentioned above. There was no change in the constitution of the firm caused by the death or retirement of the partners. It could not be said that there was any succession within the meaning of section 26(2). [107 F H] Commissioner of income tax, Madras vs P, It was held that as a result of the instrument of February 7, 1948, the business carried on by the firm of Nagjee Purushotham and Company as then constituted as bankers, piece goods and yarn merchants and as soap and cloak manufacturers and sellers. The appellant could not claim any benefit under section 25 (1). [108 G H] Figgsies ' case, referred to.

The appellant, a retired employee of the respondent Corporation, was appointed as Assistant Branch Manager (Admn.) in 1963. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that the transfer of the appellant from Class III to Class IV and Class IV employees became void because the appellant had not passed through a class II post after 1st September, 1956. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The transfer of an employee from Class I to Class III and ClassIV posts in Class IV is made by the Corporation on that day in the Central Government and providing for its management. [200E] (2) The Transfer of the employees of insurers as the age of superannuation in some of the companies was sixty and not to derive benefit from expertise and experience of employees who had worked with insurers. It suggests that the transferred employees are always amenable for separate treatment and they do not lose their identity. Aneja vs Union of India and Others, [Civil Writ No. 1987 in which the validity o f the continua tion of some foreign Air Hostesses beyond the prescribed age of retirement came up for consideration. A ministerial railway servant who entered Government service on or before the 31st March, 1938 and held on that date (i) a lien or a suspended lien on a permanent post, or 219 (ii) a temporary post in a provision al substantive capacity under Clause (d) of Rule 2008 and continued to hold the same without interruption until he was confirmed in that post, shall be retained in service till the day he attains the age Of sixty years subject again to the power of the Corporation to retire any such employee on completion of 55 years of age or at any time thereafter if his efficiency was found to have been impaired. [201B C] (3) The Regulation 19 framed by the corporation under the second limb of sub section (2A) of Section 49 of the Act is not inconsistent with the Act and the rules made thereunder. [202G H] (4) The appellant, an employee of a Corporation, who entered service on 1st October, 1938, and held in that date was entitled to continue in service until they were duly altered by the Central Govern ment. [203C D] (5) The provisions of sub sections (2 A) and (2B) of section 49 of Act are not inconsistent therewith. It is only in respect of transferred employees being struck down on the ground that it violates the equality provisions of Part 111 of the Constitution because similar action has not been taken in respect o newly recruited employees. [204D] (6) The power to make regulations not inconsistentwith the Act or the rules framed thereunder, is subject to the control of the Central Gover nment and the Corporation is entitled to appoint them in its service by the Order of the State Government dated 25th February, 1964.

The appellants, who were members of the Bar belonging to the District Bar Association, Bhiwani, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Punjab and Haryana High Court (Punjab and Haryana) Rules, 1974. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the letters written by the appellants were correct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letter did not interfere much less substantial ly with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the courts. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High. Court proceeded on the basis that the Letters Patent Bench had no jurisdiction to entertain the contempt proceedings. [244E] 1.2 It is a conditional apology. The Full Bench fell into the error of accepting the apology without finding that the appellants committed any contempt. [245G] 2.1 In any case, if in view of this Hon 'ble Court, the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. The reasons are obvious. It will not be correct and proper for any Judge to accept the invitation and hospitality of any busi ness or commercial organisation or of any political party or of a club or organisation run on sectarian, communal or parochial lines. [246B] 2:2 In any event if in spite of this Court 's order the action is not brought within the ambit of contempt of Court, one will be more than the functionary himself. [247C D] 3.1 It will also not be wrong and proper to any Judge accept the offer and hpersonalospitality of a busi cess or Commercial organisation or any political con stent organisation run by sectarian. The reason is obvious. If on facts it appears that the Judge did say things or matters about politics such utterances or views or observations will be the personal opinions expressed by the Judge, and, therefore, the protec tive umbrella of the court cannot be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt. It is necessary to state here that if on facts there is no allegation of contempt, one may be more a sorry but the deponent itself. [248D] 3:2 The High ' Court proceeded upon the basis as if the appellants had committed any Contempt.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and it was carrying on business in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. to the Investigation Commission appointed under the , and it had been constituted under the . The petitioner company had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1954 55. On the 12th April, 1954, the Central Government issued a notification under section 5(1) of the Indian Income tax Act declaring that certain persons were liable to pay tax on profits and gains arising from business carried on by it in the course of its business. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court which dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of sections 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Act had become void as being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the Constitution of India. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner company that (i) the provisions Of section 5 of the , were not violative of article 14 of the constitution inasmuch as they gave arbitrary power to the Commission to pick and choose and secondly because the clause was highly discriminatory in nature, the same had become invalid; (ii) the proviso to sub section (4) of section 7 of the impugned Act did not apply to the facts of the case inasmuch as the provisions were not discriminatory in so far as it gave arbitrary powers to the Central Commission to take action against the petitioner under the provisions. HELD: (i)(a) The provisions of section 5 are not violative Of article 14 and are, therefore, void because they give arbitrary power on the part of the Commission which is a judicial proceeding and all the incidents of such judicial proceedings have to be observed before the result is arrived at; (b) The impugned Act does not contravene article 14 inasmuch as it gives arbitrary powers on the Commission under section 34 of the Income tax law. [457 D E] (ii)(a). It is clear that if persons dealt with by the impugned act are deprived of the substantial and valuable privileges which they would otherwise have if they were dealt with under the Act, in that situation it is no defence to say that the discriminatory procedure also advances the course Of justice. [454 F G] (b)(i) The words "any person" occurring in section 5 must be read as including a person who is not by nature, attainment or circumstance, in the same position. It is well settled that if a person dealt with in the Indian income tax Act is deprived of his substantial and precious privileges which he would otherwise had if they had been dealt with Under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, or any other law, he would certainly be entitled to have his case considered under section 4(4) and (7).

The appellants, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, were carrying on business in shop, commercial establishment, establishments for public entertainment or amusement and other establishments. The Federation was incorporated under section 26 of the Indian companies Act, 1956. It had its registered office at Delhi. In the course of trade, industry or transport or other business matters, and to secure the services of expert technical men (vide clauses (f) and (k) of the Memorandum of Association). The appellants were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling articles and commodities. They were carrying out activities for the purpose of securing organised action on all subjects mentioned above. In respect of disputes arising between them, the Federation filed a suit in the Court of Chief Judge, Delhi, claiming that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2(9) of Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the premises in which the registered office of the Federation is located was not a commercial establishment within the meaning of section 2 (5) of that Act and that it had no application. It also held that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under section 10(1)(c) of Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that it fell within part (b) of section 10 (1)(d) of income tax Act, 1922. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that before the High Court, at no stage, it had been urged on behalf Of the Federation that the activity of the Association carried on in the premises was a business or trade and business. It was further submitted that the activities of the association were not a "commercial establishment" within the definition of " commercial establishment" as given in section 3(5) (b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The activity of a Federation is one of general utility; the only source of its income is from subscriptions. It helps businessmen and industrialists by securing for them the services Of expert technical man (vide clause (k), of the memorandum of Association); and no portion thereof shall be paid or transferred directly or indirectly, by way of dividend, bonus or otherwise by way profit to the members of the federation. [353 D] 1.2 The activity carried on by a company is one which is engaged in trade and commerce. It deals with the trade or busi ness in general to secure its interest for the benefit of the country. It does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. [352 A B] 1:3 In the instant case, the activity carried out in the shop was a "business" and "shop" in section 11 of the Act. [355 E F] 2.1 In the matter of Incorporated Council of Law Reporting for England and Wales, (1) the Queens Bench was considering the interpretation of the expression "commercial Establishment" inasmuch as its activities were connected with trade and industry generally. The entire case law was surveyed. It is predominantly a charitable organization and not a professional one. [356 G H] 2:2 In the present case, it is predominantly an 'commercial establishment ' and not "shops" which are engaged in business or commerce. Therefore, the activities carried on were business and material services rendered to businessmen, traders and industrialist who are members of constituents of the Union. The activity was one of a general utility. It has been done in the interest of trade and trade.

The dispute between the Jagirdars and Zamindars ultimately ended in 1837 by a compromise between the British Government and the then Jagirdar Hat Narain Singh whereby the British government granted a pension of Rs. 36,322/8/ to Babu Ram Gopal Singh who was in turn given the Jagir. The appellant contended that the amount which had been received by the successors of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year and therefore it fell within the definition of agricultural income under section 2(1) of the Income tax Act. Held, that the allowance varied from time to year. The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1838 and, therefore, it was not agricultural income as defined in the Act. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa (2) and MaharajadhanhirajaSir Kameshwar Singh 's case ([1924] I T.C.R. 325), distinguished. The allowance varied by year to years and the source of the income still remains the arrangement and not land. The character of the payment is again not the same as the character in which it was received by him as trustee. It seems to us that in this case the source from which the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of the rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of his income still remained the arrangement. The nature of the allowance is also different if he exchanges (1) 30 T. C. 325, (2 ) 31 T.T.R., 325, and (3) 705 the words "pension allowances or Malikana" in the letter dated July 7, 1837, and determine the real character of payment.

The appellants of Civil Appeal No. Sd/ K.G.O.F., who had been promoted as Chargeman II on completion of 2 years ' satisfactory service could be promoted by following the procedure contemplated by Rule 8 of the Madhya Pradesh Ordnance Factories (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1960. It was also apparent from the said judgment that though a right to be considered for prom o tion is a condition of service, mere chances of promoti on are not. The only effect of t he circular dated 20th Januar y, 1966 stood that Supervisors A ' on completion o f 2 years' satisfactory service would be promoted to next higher post in accordance with the normal rules i.e. on the principle of seniority cum fitness. [441F] 1:3 It is not a fit case for initiating any proceedings for contempt again st the respondents. The same view was reiterated in Mohammad Shujat Ali & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors, ; , and M/s. Ram Kumar & Co., (P) Ltd. vs State of Haryana & Ors; , referred to. 1:4 In the instant case, the appellants were not promoted as Supervisor Grade II after completion of two years ' service. The circular also did not contain any provision for promotion to the posts of Charge man II on provi sion basis. The appellant, a cinema theatre belonging originally to Messrs. Faraqui and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled under the agreement dated November 27, 1954 to exhibit cinematograph films in the theatre. The trial court held that the parties had failed to prove that the agreement between them was not genuine and that the suit was barred by res judicata. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and remanded the case for fresh disposal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the consent decree was not a matter to be decided by the Court; (ii) the question asked in cross examination of the witnesses for Filmistan intended to secure disclosure of the surrounding circumstances and conduct of the parties in order to show in what manner the language of the document was related to the existing facts could not be excluded. HELD : (i ) The consent decree must be held to create a bar of res judicata as far as the question of document of November 27 1954, creatin g a lease is concerned; and (ii ) the Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issue of resjudicata or any other issue. [417 D] (i)(a) The consent order must be set aside and the Trial Court should proceed and dispose of the suit. [404 C] (b) In a case where the court has decided the question whether in fact the subordinate Court had decided the matter of res jurisdiction, then the Court has no jurisdiction on principles of res estoppel to go into that question or to decide that question over again to the extent to which the Court, viz., the trial Court in the instant case, proposed to go to that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1, 1960. [405 D] Major section Khanna vs Brig. To interpret the expression "case" as an entire proceeding only and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved litigant where it is most needed and may results in some cases in denial of relief to him where it was most needed. Exercise of the power is broadly subject to three important conditions (1) that the decision is of a Court subordinate to the High court; (2) that there is an adjudication by the court which, viz. the trial Judge in the present case, propose to go on that question; and the High Courts proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Judge, and which could not have been decided by it until the parties were opportunity to lead evidence thereon. [414 E F] (ii)(a). The Court gave a finding expressly and by implication, on the issues of res bar, that the jurisdiction of the Court of mall Causes to decide disputes between a tenant and his landlord and falling within the purview of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act is derived from section 28. [416 F] Major Section Khanna vs Col. To construe the expression 'case" in section 28(1) of the Act, but at the same time if an issue is in fact barred by Res judicata, then it is proposing to exercise the jurisdiction which is not vested in it by law. Exercise Of the power was broadly subject only to three essential conditions (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). The order passed by the High courts is set aside.

[723B] 1.2 In the instant case, the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character. It stems out of the fundamental principle of our criminal jurisprudence that the accused is entitled to the benefit of any reasonable doubt. To entitle an accused person to the benefits of a doubt arising from the possibility of a duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him. [758E F] 1:3 The principles are now well settled. R. Occasionally phrases like 'manifestly illegal ', grossly unjust ' have been used to describe the orders of acquittal which warrant interference. To enable entitle an appellant to the advantage of a presumption arising from possibility of duality, the probable view in respect of his possible view must beas nearly reasonably possible as that Against him. "A reasonable doubt", it has been remarked, "does not mean some light, airy, insubstantial doubt that may flit through the minds of any of us about almost anything at some time or other, it does not mean a doubt begotten by sympathy out of reluctance to convict; it means a real doubt, a doubt founded upon reason"(4). (5) A reasonable doubt" is an imaginary doubt, founded upon reasons"(6). (724B C] 1 :8. Where the Trial Court allows itself to be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects creditworthy evidence for slender reasons and takes a view of the evidence which is but barely possible, it is the obvious duty of the High Court to interfere in the interest of justice, lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule. [759D] 1.:9. The principles laid down by this Court are now firmly settled. [761F] 2:10. In the present case, there was no evidence that the appellant had any deep motive to kill the deceased. It is true that the incident happened in the middle of the night and it took place at about one and a half years before the occurrence. The accused did not have any deep reason to kill his wife. He felt giddy and was about to lose consciousness. W. They caught hold of the deceased with a knife in his hand. The appellant was about loosing consciousness. The deceased intervened and interposed herself between P.Ws. 1 and 2. The house consisted of only one room. One room was also there. There was an altercation. The incident happened at about 5 A.15. When the Police officers went to the village, they found that the deceased was sleeping in a room.
