The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 1,04,682. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The object of section 24(1) is to allow a set off of profits against losses arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 24 (2). [258 A] (2) The proviso in dispute there are no positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head business. It carves out an exception to the main provision to which it has been enacted as a proviso and to no other. [258 B C] (3) The true meaning of the word "total world income" is that it qualifies the generality of the main enactment, by providing an exception and taking out as it were, from the main enacting, a portion which, but for the proviso would fall within the main clause. Therefore it is to be construed harmoniously with the main object (Per Das, C. J., dissenting) (4) The word " total world income ' in section 24 of the Indian Act does not distinguish between business in British India or business in an Indian State or so divide business. [259 D] (5) The expression "total net world income " in section 25(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922, is used in a restricted sense and takes within its sweep all profits arising from the business carried on by the assessee. It does not mean that it applies only to those profits which are attributable to the business of an assessee.

The appellant company was converted into a Public Limited Company. It had branches in Bombay and Madras. The general practice of the Company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appears to have been to fix the retirement age at 60 years, that is, between 1952 and 1961. In some cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In certain cases the company had branches at Bombay and Via Madras. In several of these matters the Company had adopted a practice in comparable concerns in Bombay region to fix their retirement age. The Company contended that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age of 58 subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. Held, that the Tribunal had erred in making these observations and the Tribunal should have made those pronouncements. The Tribunal was right in holding that the trend in Bombay regions had been to fixing the age at 58 and not at 60. The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are, in our opinion, wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. In the instant case an attempt appears to be made on behalf of the respondent Company to show that it is not correct to say that the error in fixing the retirement Age at 60 was incorrect. The fact that the company has adopted a uniform practice in similar concerns in the neighbourhood in recent times, cannot justify the inference that the decision in Bombay Region had been correctly taken by this Court in Dunzop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs The Workmen, ; , followed.

The appellants were appointed Managing Director of the Company from December 5, 1961 and their remuneration was approved by the Central Government on July 30, 1962. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order declaring that the affairs of the company were being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the shareholders for whom it was difficult,to get together and take steps for the protection of their interests jointly. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the formation of an opinion by the Board is intended to be subjective and if the provision is constitutional which in our view is the question would arise: what is about which the Board was entitled to form an opinion? Held, that the power conferred on the Central Govern ment under section 237(b) of the Act is administrative and not judicial since 323 its exercise one way or the other does not affect the rights of a company nor does it lead to any serious consequences as, for instance, hampering the business of the Board. The power to call for information is conferred on an authority which is not invested with the discretion of the Central government but is exercised by the Chairman of the Committee and is no more than its agent. The powers conferred upon the Central Gover ment under sections 10 E and 637 are administrative and cannot be delegated to any other person or persons. The Board acts in the name of the Secretary Company Law Board, May 19, 1965, (purporting to be under section 236(b). The power conferred to order an investigation is administrative but not judicial because it is the function of the Chairman to decide whether a particular thing is necessary for the purpose of the inquiry. The discretion conferred on him by section 237 is administrative. It does not lead to serious consequences and as such the exercise of one way may or the others do not affect any rights of the other.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to three years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances do not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before us. HELD: The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. [20G H] In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case.(In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. Even then, we think that the time gap is too long for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away.) [20H] In the present cases, the time interval between 19 days and August 17, 1962 was too short for original offences to have disposal of the properties to these appellant Or to had left the property in their possession till suchtime as the old offenders could have taken them away. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him.

The petitioners, who were owners of certain poisons and regulated by the Delhi Poison Act, 1904, were contending that in substance manufactured by them did not come within Rule 2(x)(2) and there were some correspondence in this regard. When the competent authority held that the substance manufactured was poison for purposes of the Act, the petitioners did not question the finding on any material. The petitioners contended that though the Act is a Central enactment it is possible to include substance as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance as medicine is not automatically made applicable to the other States. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of 'thinner ' contained in Rule 2 (x)(ii) of the Rules is not exhaustive but only illustrative and exhaustive. It would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [223A B] 1.2 In order to determine what substance they would include as poison, it is necessary to consider whether the substance would come within the definition of "thinetency" mentioned in Rule 3(x) of Rules. The word 'poison ' has been defined in Rule 4 of the rules which reads as under: "Any substance specified as a poison in a rule made or notification issued under this Act shall be deemed to be a poison for the purpose of this Act". [223C D] 1:3 In many cases deaths have also occurred due to drinking such substance. The definition is not inclusive but exhaustive. The expression 'poisons ' has not been defined anywhere in the Rules. It is only those substances which are used for purposes mentioned therein can certainly be declared as poison. [224D E] 2.1 In many instances deaths have occurred due t o drinking such substances. Nothing is a poison unless regard be had to its administration. The substance which is used for purpose mentioned therein cannot definitely be declared to be poison. It may also be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. [225F G] 2:2 In many such cases deaths had also occurred owing to drinking Such substance. Nothing was a poison which is intended for purposes o f the Act. It was used for purging such substance by the time or manner of their adminis tration. The use of the word 'population ' in Rule 5(x), therefore, would not make any difference. [226F G; 227A B]. 2:3 The definition given to the word "poison" in Rule 1(x ) (ii) is wide enough to include all substances which can be termed as poison for purpose of the act. [227C D]. 2.4 In many other cases deaths having occurred due lo drinking such material, the Govern ment consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulat ed in the interest of health and security of the society. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to a word poison. But under this term would fall anything calcu lated to destroy life.

The appellants were partners of a firm registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The firm was carrying on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. In the assessment for income tax of the appellants for the assessment year 1952 53 relevant to the account year Samvat 417 2007 all item of Rs. 2,68,385/ due from the Bombay firm at the foot of their running account as a bad debt written off as irrecoverable. The Income Tax Officer held that the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in the assessee 's money lending business nor a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. On appeal by the Department to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal rejected the application but pursuant to an order made by the High Court under section 66(2) submitted a supplementary statement of the case on the following question "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the ease the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debts of Rs 2, 68,385 were not bad and bad debt in law ?" The High Court rejected the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the debt or any part thereof is in respect of loans made in the ordinary course of business by a money lender; it may be wholly unrelated to the business of the tax payer; and (ii) the amount actually written off is not in respect Of loans made by a loan. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question framed at 422 the instance of the High court did not bring out the real question arising for decision. [445C] 2.1 In order to answer the question reframed it must be shown that the conclusion reached by the Tribunal is not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. It is true as contended by the learned Counsel for the appellant, that the conclusions reached by it are not supported with proper discussion or facts of the statement. But that statement merely catalogued the arguments advanced at the bar. The failure to adjust interest in the account of the Bombay Firm at the stage at which it became a debtor in Samvat year 2007, the manner in which the partner of the assessee tried to explain the position in March, 1954 and the stand of the firm itself at all earlier stages support the case of the Department. [467D] 2:2 The conclusion reached on the question whether the debt is not a good or doubtful debt is allowable under section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian income tax Act. [468F] 3.1 The fact that the advances made by them to the Bombayfirm were not in the nature of loan, does not make any difference to the conclusion arrived at by the tribunal. It may be an advance the money lending or other business of a assessee but not in its nature as a loan representing loss incurred in the latter business. [469B] 3:2 In view of this finding, which is binding on this Court, it must follow that the question framed before the Tribunal did not come out for decision and the High 'Court was right. [470C D] 4.3 The conclusion arrived by the Income tax Officer from which it may have been inferred that the loans were not made in respect thereof of loans in the normal course of the business transactions, does no longer be a good proposition to hold that the amount paid by the appellants to the Madras firm was not an income chargeable under section 11(2). [470B] 5.3 In view Of this finding which is based on proper discussion and the conclusion drawn by the Appellate Tribunal, it cannot be said that there are two important circumstances which appear from the order of the Appellate Asstt.

Leave granted. The petitioners in these petitions are the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976 (hereinafter referred to as "the Bangalore Act"). Under the provisions Of Section 36 of the Karnataka Act, where the acquisitions, otherwise than by agreement, it will be regulated by the provisions , as far they are applicable. The Special Leave Petitions filed against the decision of a learned Single Judge of that High Court were dismissed on October 6, 1989. In these petitions, the petitioners have challenged the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the awards in these cases had not been made within two years from September 20, 1984. On December 16, 1987, the respondents obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question. The Petitioners in these Petitions are the owner of certain land which was acquired by them under the Land Acquisition Act. Under the Karnataka Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, Section 11 A of the Land acquisition Act, 1894, was amended by the Bangalore City Development Authority (Amendment), 1984, and thereafter by the Amendment Act, 1985. The respondents in these writ petitions are owners of some lands which had been acquired by a notification under Section 4 of the said Act. In the Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985, the Karnataka High Court granted interim stay of dispossession therein. On September 30th December, 1984 the petitioners obtained an Interim order from the Bangalore High Court directing Status quo with respect to the land in question in Special Leave petition No.294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the State Government dated August 14, 1984 and that if no award was made within that period, the entire proceedings for acqui sation of the land shall lapse. The Karnataka Land Acquis tive Authority (Acquisition) Act 1976 came into force on September 20.1984. Under Section 36(1)(b), the Collector must make his award within two year from the date of the publication of the declaration under Section 6 of the Act and that, if no Award was made before that period the entire proceeding for acquisi tion of the acquired land shall lapsed. The Bangalore Development Authority issued a notification on September 30, 1984 under Section 11A(1) of the 1894 Act in respect of certain properties which were not covered by the declaration dated September 20; 1977. On October 29, 1987 the petitioners filed Writ Petitions before the Karnataka high Court challenging the acquisition on the grounds that as the awards had not yet been made, they had lapsed. That contention was negatived along with some other contentions in the judgment of the High Court which is sought to be impugned before this Court. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [501B] 2. In view of the provisions contained in Section 11(A) of Land Acquisition Acqui sion Act, the proceedings for acquisition of the aforesaid lands had lapsed and the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 136 of the Constitution. [602C D] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the interim orders passed by this Court on October 29. 1988 directing statusquo with regard thereto had a direct impact on the determination of these Special Leave petitions. [643E] 4. In order to appreciate the question whether the stay orders were highly material in the determination o f the Special leave Petitions, it is necessary to consider the relevant dates which have to be borne in mind in this connection. The notification making the declaration was made on September 10, 1984 by the Land Acqary Authority ( Acquisition) Act. It was published on September 11, 1985 and thereafter under the Amendment Acts, 1985, Section11 A of Land acquisition (Amendment ) Act,1985 was amended.

The appellant bank was governed by the provisions of the Sastry award as modified and were not entitled to any increment in accordance with rule 4(a) of the Desai Award. The workmen entered service before January 1, 1959, and the fitment of these workmen was dealt with in para. 5. It divided the employees of the banks with which it was concerned in two groups. The second group consisted of workmen who on January 1 1962 were employed in banks which were not governed by any provisions of Chapter VA of the present Sastry award. As to the third group, the Desai award provided that these employees would first be fitted in the new scales of pay provided by the Sastry Award as laid down in para 5. 355 and 166 of the Labour Appellate Tribunal 's decision in Prakash Chand Mehra 's case (1). The workmen on January 2, 1962 were paid Rs. 175 per month as salary for each year. On February 1, 1962, the appellant bank raised a dispute before the Industrial Tribunal that they were entitled to what was provided by sub cl. (d) and that it did not matter whether what was thus arrived at exceeded the maximum provided under cl. 5 of the award. The Industrial Tribunal held that the workmen on the other hand claimed that they had been given increments in accordance therewith as modified by the Desai awards as modified, and that the fitment was made under sub cl.(d) read with sub cl (b) of el. (a) and (c), and that they could not claim any increment for 1951 and 1952, and held that they would be fitted into the new scale of pay. The appellant bank appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The Industrial Disputes Tribunal was right in holding that the Sastry awards were modified under sub clauses (d), (b), (c) and cl. 4A of el.(a) read along with sub cls. (b). [293 C] (ii) The award provided for payment of annual increments in respect of each case. It did not amount to a reduction in the scale of wages or any other benefit which could be claimed by the workmen under sub clause (d). [294 D] (iii) The Sastry Award was modified under cl.(b) readwith sub cl, (c). The award did not provide for payment for any increment. It was only for payment to the workmen who were entitled under sub cls.(a), (e) and(f) of cl. 6.

The Zoo was granted a lease of the land in question for a period of five years. The lease deed provided that the lessee would be entitled to the full amount of the lease rent at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per annum from the date of expiry of the term of the licence. The appellant 's case is that the Zoo had no right to sell the land for a further period of 5 years and that the lease deed was executed in favour of the appellant on February 12, 1981. The Government of West Bengal issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (the Act) on June 11, 1981 whereby the Government had agreed to the proposal to construct a hotel on land belonging to the Zoological Garden and that alternate arrangements were made for shifting the existing structures which were necessary for the Zo environment from the plot in question to the adjacent plot. The notification was published in the Gazette on July 1, 1982. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on various grounds including that the Government was not competent to issue a notification in terms of section 4 (1) (a) of that Act and that it had no power to issue such a notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification issued by the Government under section4(1)(a) was invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of para graphs 166 and 167 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appellant had no locus standi to file a writ petition in the High Court since he had not been impleaded as a party to the proceedings; that the order passed by the High court was without jurisdiction because the appellant did not mention what he had in mind when he spoke of a high rise building, and that he did not care. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Government is entitled to allot the land to the Taj Group of Hotels determined to give the land on lease to the appellant. [501B] 1.2 The purpose of the ZOO was to provide for the construction of a hotel in the remaining extent of Begumbari land to its members and to ensure that the facilities are available in the adjacent plots of land. It is not necessary that the State should be impleaded as party to any proceedings before the High Courts or the authorities of the Alipore Zoologyogical Garden, but it is only when the State makes available to this court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the State Government land to respondent No. 1. [525C] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant was not impleaded as an party to proceedings before any High Court or authorities of that Zoo and its inmates. The fact that he had no interest in the land at all could not be said to have been suppressed by him when he speaks of a low rise building. [500D] 2:2 The Government was entitled to allotment of land to Taj Group for a larger period of time than the one which the ZO had in view while granting the lease. It was not necessary to mention that the Chief Minister turned a blind eye and a dent ear ear to the interests and the requirements for the zoo animals and also hampering the beauty of the zoological Park determined to giving the land, to them and with a mind closed to every thing else. [511F] 2 :3 The Government had no authority to issue any notification in exercise of its power under section 3(1). It was only when it decided to grant the lease that the land would be required for a public purpose.

The assessee company was incorporated in the year 1957. The assessee company had a cash balance of Rs.4000 only on 1.1.1957 and it did not have any overdraft facilities with any bank. The Income Tax Officer, by his letter dated 1.2.1957, asked the assessee to send his father, a partner of the firm for the gift of Rs 25,000 made in favour of his son Pravin. The appellant company contended that the said sum was available with the said firm of M/s Pearls & Beads and that there was no evidence that Tika Ram and Sons were carrying on any banking business. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee 's contention holding that the transfer evidenced by the entries in the books of account and by the declaration, did not operate to bring into existence a valid gift. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee company could not be said to have made gifts in cash of the amounts credited in favour Of his wife and relatives. The Revenue appealed to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the donor by reason of which he could make the gift by such book entries. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that a total sum of Rs,000 was available in the hands of the donees was Rs.81,000 and cash balance with firm was only Rs.4,299 but the unuti lised overdraft of the Firm was Rs,4, 299, but there was nothing to show that the amount was available for the purpose of investment or benefit by the donor or permitting the doner to share them out of the bundle or rights gifted in the proper ty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether a gift is made by transfer en ments in the book of account or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [130E] 2.1 In the instant case before us and the High Courts have rightly held that there had been no evidence to support the claim of the assessee that the transaction in question was bona fide but dismissed the appeal of the Revenue on the sole ground that the transfers evidenced by entries in books of accounts and by declaration did not affect the character of the gift. [131F] 2:2 The High Courts were in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [132B] 3.1 There was no proof, even oral instructions, that the transactions in question were bona fide and the firms where accounts transfer are effected have overdraft facilities. The entries in these books did not complete the gift but only oral instructions were said to be given. There was nothing on record to show as to how the transaction was bona bonafide. [133C] 3:2 In the case of banking companies or other firms, who have overdraft facility even if the sums are not in credit of the donee and are not with such companies or firms, gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries.[132D] 4.1 The High court was in error while answering the questions in the affirmative. [134E] 5.2 In view of the fact that the property was gifted by a donor the possession and enjoyment of which was allowed to a partnership firm in which the donor was a partner, then the mere fact of the dont sharing the enjoy ment or the benefit in the property is not sufficient for the application of section 10 of the , until and unless such enjoyment or benefit was clearly referable to the gift, i.e. to the parting with such enjoy ment/ benefit by donee or permitting his doner or permit the doners to share their out of bundle or right gifted in such property.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service Rules 1963, framed under the Orissa Superior judicial Service Rules, 1963, provided that the Governor may appoint a person to be and to fill up such posts. The rules of recruitment to the post of District Judges were made by the Governor in consultation with the High Court. The Governor promulgated the Orissa Higher Judicial Service Act 1963, on March 6, 1967, which was published in the Gazette on September 21, 1966. By an order dated October 10, 1966, the Governor promulgated Orissa SuperiorJudicial Service Rules 1964, and directed that the said rules be amended accordingly. In pursuance of this order, the State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act appointing the secretaries to the government of Orissa. The High Court held that the power to transfer the district judges and addl. district judges from one post to another whether as a judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands, and that the Government had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the Government of Orissa, and dismissed the writ petition filed by the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High court was right in holding that the powers to transfer District Judges from one district to another were included in the 'control ' exercisable by the High Courts over district courts under article 235, or in the power of 'appointment of persons to be or the posting and promotion, of district judges ' which is to be exercised by the Government under article 233, though in consultation, with the Chief Justice of Orissa the Governor could appoint a District Judge. HELD: (1) The High court must also have the power under article 227 to direct that any officer appointed to the service of a district shall be transferred from one place to another. [164 D] (2) The power to appoint a district judge is not included in his 'control " exercisable by him over district court" within the meaning of article 235. [165 E F] (3) The expression 'control over district Court ' in article 235 means that the control over district judiciary must be exercised on the basis of the policy displayed by the Constitution and not on the ground that it is necessary to fillup those posts.

The appellant, a co sharer, was the owner of agricultural land in village Kherra, District Ambala. The suit land belonged to more than one co sharers and had not been sold jointly by all the co shar er. The respondent No. 1, who owned the land or property sold or a part thereof, filed a suit for pre emption under section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Preemption Act 1913, alleging that the appellant was in possession of the land since long and had been cultivating the same jointly with his father and brother. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1) (f) of Constitution. On appeal by the respondent No 1, the High Court upheld the validity holding that the right of pre emation conferred on co sharpers as well as to a tenant could be justified as they constitute a class by themselves. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The right of preemption based on consanguinity was held to be a relic of the feudal past totally inconsistent with the constitutional philosophy and scheme. [125B] In the instant case also the appellant seeks to exercise the right under clause 'fourthly '; of section 15 (1)(b) of Punjab Pre emption Act 1913 before its amendment in 1960, in order of succession. The right conferred on a cosharer was upheld on the consideration that if an outsider is introduced as a co tenant in a property it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. [126F G] In view of the fact that the suit land belongs to more or less than one family, the appellant cannot claim pre emention under clause `fourthly ". The expression 'other co sharants ' in section 15 is wide enough to include all co shars who do not fail under clause (1) First or 'Secondly ' or 'Thirdly ' of Section 15(2)(b). [126H; 127A] In order to claim pre mption the right owes statutorily fixed and even in the case of those falling within the same class, the right has been regulated by the use of the expression, 'in order of inheritance '. The rights of preemption conferred on tenants as well to a co cos sharer were upheld as reasonable and in public interest.

The petitioner, a widow of one K.V Seshiah married two wives. The adoptive mother died on 21.8.1987 and the adoptive mother filed a petition for compromise in respect of the entire subject matter of litigation. The alienees had also taken such stand in the litigation. In February 1985, during the pendency of the special leave petition the adoptive father died. With the death of the adoptive parents, Seshiraj led claim to the entire property as heir. While each of the parties had taken such stands in the litigations a compromise was brought about on 21 8.1987 between the father and his two sons and the same was filed in this Court. The terms of the compromise stipulated payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the father to each of his two daughters in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. When the matter was listed before the Court for recording the compromise, Sudarshan Gupta, second respondent herein, maintained that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The alienation was for about a purported consideration of Rs 1 lakh each and the second and third respondents have received the same. In the face of such a statement in the compromise deed signed by the parties the second respondent had disputed the fact of payment and has, in the meantime, alienated about 81 acres of property which constitutes the subject matter o dispute to third parties. The alienations are for about Rs. 81 acres and have even maintained that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise and we must hold that there have been improvements of the property by the alienees. The transferees have also been maintaining that there had been improvements in the property prior to 21.08.1987. In view of such an statement in this compromise deed, the second Respondent had disputed his fact of payments and has even maintained the document of compromise to be genuine. The assignees have also accepted the fact that some improvements have been made to the property which too we have not gone into, they have no interest in the aforesaid property. The purchasers have also admitted the fact regarding payment and have also maintained that the alienation is for about 3 years old by now. In these circumstances, the alienee respondent No. 2 had no right created under the alleged sale deeds. They have also denied the fact about improvements made to them by the petitioner. The sales are pendente lite. The transfers are pendente se lite. In this view of the matter, the alienations are not for about an indefinite consideration and they cannot be acted upon. The High Court has rightly held that the alienes had no interest created under alleged sale deed prior to its compromise and they have even maintain that there has been improvements made by the assignees. The transactions are pendente hoc. In fact, if the compromise is valid and binding the alienor respondent No 2 had any interest in his property prior before the compromise for which there was no acceptable evidence. The reversionees have accepted the document as genuine. They also admitted that they had not received the sum of Rs,1 lakh from the date of the sales which is more than three years old. In such a situation, the alienation would be valid and enforceable and the transferees have become owners of the properties and has only maintained that they have since been in possession of the land from the day of the sale which is less than three year ' old by then. The transfer deeds are for a purported Consideration of Rs 2 lakhs and Rs.77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents have been paid before the registering authority. The transfereeees have also not challenged the fact as to why the compromise should not be acted on and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. The factum of compromise is not in dispute.

The workmen of the Company, who were employed in the respondent company, were granted sick leave for a period of 15 days. The Company applied for and obtained special leave to appeal as aforesaid, with the further direction that the appeal may be heard along with the identical matter (in the Alembic Glass Industries case) except the identical matters, the workmen would receive more wages by remaining absent than on duty. The Tribunal gave its award dated Septem ber 24, 1975 in the case of the Alemmbic glass Indus tries case, except that the direction regarding 7 days sick leave was given retrospective effect from January 1, 1975. The company applied for special leave as aforesaid and obtained Special Leave to appeal against the same. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days ' sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. [729G] (2) The benefit of sick leave is therefore lost when the Act was made applicable to the region from December 14, 1969. [761B] (3) The benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave to the workmen of those companies are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's awards in that respect. [762D] (4) The award in the present case was on the lines of the earlier award in a case like the present for examining any controversy regarding the work man 's demands for additional benefits, but it has been argued by the learned counsel for the appellants that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to give relief to the workers of those two companies.

The appellant was detained under the order of detention passed by the Government of Bombay on 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were vague and the last two have been urged before us not only as independent points but as reinforcing the first two. The High Court directed that the return forthwith of all papers and articles seized should be furnished at Bombay. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the detaining authority was acting otherwise than bona fide, and (2) the material was not enough to enable him to make a representation against the order under which he was detained. HELD: (i) The right of a detenue under article 22(5) includes two distinct components. It is well settled that the authority is under a constitutional obligation to furnish reasonably definite grounds, as well as adequate particulars then and there or shortly thereafter. [384B C] (ii)The authority is not under a Constitutional obligation to disclose facts considered against public interest. The authority is in a constitutional duty to furnish fairly definite grounds for his detention. It follows that the detaining authorities are claiming privilege or applying its mind to the question of privilege. [386E F] (iii)The right of representation guaranteed by article 22 (5) comprises two distinct elements. It includes both the existence of the authority and the effect of the order. The power not to disclose information in the affidavit of the Under Secretary indicated a decision for nondisclosure, by the Under secretary himself and that too at the time of filing the affidavit. Bambawala to suggest that it is now that the detention authority is claiming privilege and applying its minds to the questions of privilege, cannot be implied in these circumstances. [387B C D] (iv)The detaining authority is entitled to make an effective representation against his order under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. The right to make such a representation is not absolute or conditional. It does not include the right to know the grounds on which it is based. [388C E] (v)The power notto disclose facts referred to in the grounds of the detention cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of the detenue for being afforded a proper opportunity of representation. The detaining authority has been given an opportunity of making a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section10 of the . [388B C]. (vi)The order of release is not vitiated by any infirmity or illegality in the order made by the detaining Authority. It was therefore necessary to have an idea of the grounds and consideration of the question as submitted.

The respondent was a minor. He was dismissed from service by the Central Government under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r.14 of the said Rules was ultra vires the . Held, that the rule was intra vires the , Rao has no case. The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes it clear that the rules framed under section 191 of the . Sub section 2(a) provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. Section 19 makes a provision for removal of an officer without being tried and convicted by court Martial. The word "subject" occurring therein in section 20 makes it abundantly clear that if the Central Govt. is satisfied or the C in C is of the opinion that the trial of the officer by a Court martial is inexpedient or impracticable, but considers the further retention of the same officer in the service as undesirable, the C shall communicate the view of the Central government or his views, as the case may be, to the officer together with all reports adverse to him and he shall be called upon to submit his explanation and defence. The expression "subject lo the provisions" occurring there is no warrant for reading a rule where under, subject to the other provisions of the Act, the Central Govern ment is satisfied that the accused has committed misconduct against an officer whose further retention in service is not considered desirable.

The appellant company was granted a licence to carry on the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The company applied for the issue of a writ quashing the resolution dated February 25, 1963, passed by the Standing Committee, Zila Parishad, Nagpur, and for a writ of mandamus directing the Standing committee not to interfere with the right of the appellant to impose and collect octroi duty pursuant to its resolution dated March 25,1963. The High Court held that the Panchayat Samiti could not dismiss the appeal of the company as being barred by limitation because r.3(a) did not require the Panchayat to fix the octroi limits in the resolution passed under r. 3(a). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the bye law laid down by the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958, which authorises the levy is r.22 and therefore the Panchayat could not impose octroi duty from January 14, 1964, in accordance with the resolutions dated February 28, 1963 and March 17, 1963. HELD: (i) The rule which authorises imposition of a tax or fee is r 22 and it enjoins that the procedure prescribed in rr.3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi duty can start being levied. Rule 21 provides for refund of octroi. [221 C D] (ii) The rules which authorise the levy are r. 22 and do not require that the panchayat must fix the tax limits in accordance to r.21, and if so read, it would mean that before the Octroi duty can commence being levied, r. 21 must be complied with. [222 G H] (iii) Rule 21 does not require a Panchayat to fixing the octroi limit in the resolutions passed under rr. 3 and 4. The rule is therefore ultra vires. [223 C D].

The respondents were engaged in gold trade, i.e., manufacturers, shroffs and dealers in gold was found carrying on business as a money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business. The Administrator refused permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon him thereunder could be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to work on money lent or banking trade business on a security of some article ornament, etc. The High Court struck down sec. 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 on the grounds that it suffered from the infirmity of excessive delegated legislative power and that it was violative of Art. 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Administrator had no authority to refuse permission or grant permission. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The object of the enactment and the scheme of the Act is to ensure prevention of circumvention of other provisions of the statute and the Scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [954 G H] (2) Section 28 confers an absolute arbitrary and uncanalised powers without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The power conferred on him thereunder can be exercised by the Administrator, but that is not decisive of the matter. [1055 B D] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division while declaring unamended sec. 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. [ 1056 A C] (3) The scheme of section 28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of enactment and scheme affords sufficient guidelines to the administrator in the matters of exercising discretion under this section. It does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on moneylending, banking or any other business in the said premises in that premises in Which he carries on business but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender and banker on his security while seeking approval to carryon business as such dealer. [1156 B D]. (4) The power of the administrator under section 28 does not confer any arbitrary or uncanalised or arbitrary power upon a trader who seeks permission under this Section and give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission. [1106 C] Harkchand Ratanlal Banthia vs Asst collector of Central excise Poona, I Division while holding that sec.28 confers an unguided and uncan uncontrolled power without any guidelines for guiding its discretion by the administrator, but it does not prescribe any criteria or guideline guide lines has been imposed upon the Administration under section 5(1) of the , and gives reasons in cases he decides not to refuse to grant permission or to grant permit. [109 H] Harkrchand Ratan Chand Banthia 's case (supra) followed.

The appellants claimed that they had acquired title by adverse possession, and that the properties in question belonged to the temple. The trial court held that the alienations covered by Exts. 125 and 126 were not bona fide and that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. On appeal, the lower appellate Court held that (1) the properties covered by Ext. 125 were not the property of the deity; (2) the alienation evidenced by Exts., 125 and 127 was in favour of their predecessors in title though burdened with an obligation to render service to the matam; and (3) the alienations made by the appellants were in contravention of article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act. On a reference, the High Court held against respondents 2 & 3 that they did not acquire title by way of adverse possession before the suit was filed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the sale deeds fell within the purview of article 133 B; and that (ii) the alienors had been removed from management of the temple, and other persons had taken up the position as de facto managers, and therefore they were not entitled to possession. HELD: (1)(a) The question whether a transfer effected by the manager of a temple in regard to properties belonging to the Temple falls outside the mischief of article134 B is a mixed question of fact and law, and the High Courts were in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title of the Temple had not been lost by adverse Possession before the suits were filed. [124 D E] (b) The plea of limitation with which the Privy Council was concerned in that case was based on article 134B, and it was held that article 144 would govern such a case. [125 F G] (c) The High Court was in error by reversing the decision of the Courts below by observing that the question as to whether on facts proved in the present case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removing, is a pure question of law and fact and it does not make any difference to the application of article 136 B. [126 E] Gnanasambanda vs Damodar Das, A.I.R. 1936 Mad. 969, referred to. (2)(a). The High Courts have rightly held that in view of the decision in Gnanagambandhu vs Damodar Dass, A I. R. , the question whether on the facts proved by the evidence it could be drawn whether the previous Manager or trustee has been removed, is one which would exclude transfers made by a Shebait or a manager of the Hindu religious endowment on the basis that the property belongs not to the endowment but to the manager himself ? [127 D E]. (b). The question as regards the validity of the alienations in question was whether the alienor must be deemed to have resigned his office or left it. If there is, article 144 of the same Schedule is applicable to the property; and if there is no, article 134 A would not apply to the present ease because the alienation effected by a manager on the ground that the transferor treated the properties as his own, it does appear that the two earlier Privy Council decisions in Gnnanasadambande 's case lend some support to the contention. [127 E F] (3)(a), The question of limitation is one of fact, and law. In determining whether a suit for possession of immovable property by a reversioner or a Manager of a Hindu religious endowments was within the mischief Of article 134 C. If it is shown that the transfer is made on the other basis that it belongs to the Endowment, article 136B would not be applicable to such a suit after 12 years ' adverse possession. [128 G H] (4)

The appellant Ved Gupta decided to construct and operate an air conditioned Cinema in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. By a subsequent agreement executed by the 14 partners on February 22, 1969, the name of the cinema business was changed from 'Metro Theatre ' to 'Apsara Theatre '. The licence for running the Apsara Cinema was granted for premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the name and style of 'Apara Theatre'. Consequent thereon, the firm was reconstituted and a new partnership deed was executed by both the partners on April 11, 1970, Clause 18 of the said document contained the following recital: "The licence for run the Apara Cinema by which Apsra Theatre is being run stands in the names of Shri Ved Gupta s/o Shakur Dass, the 9th party. After considering the arguments advanced before him by the counsel appearing for the contending parties, the District Magistrate passed a detailed order dated December 29, 1977 rejecting the request of Todar Mal and Krishan Kumar and declaring Shri VedGupta to be the sole licensee authorized to run the Cinema Theatre. The appellant filed an appeal against the said order before the District Judge who dismissed the same on April 29, 1978. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the District magistrate had acted strictly in accordance with law in passing the impugned order and that the writ petition was devoid of merit. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The licence granted to Ved Gupta for running a Cinema shows in the Theatre itself that the cinema shows in its own name. So long as they did not have a licence we have already found that the licence had been granted to Todarmal only in his individual and personal capacity and not as a representative of the firm. [975F G] 1.2 The District Magistrate was therefore justified in passing an order directing the suspension of the Cinema shows from the Theatre premises. [964E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the licence for the running the cinema show in the theatre cannot be said to have been granted as a Representative of the partner who wanted to run it without a licence in contravention of the provisions of the Act and the Rules. The impugned order passed by the District Collector directing the suspending of the A para Theatre is not one suspending the licence issued in respect of the Theatre. [965G] 2:2 It is only after considering the submissions advanced before it by the appellant that the High Court had already found the licence granted in respect thereof in favour of Turi Mal and Kishan Kumar, that the impugned action was taken. The writ petitioners before the High court were some of the partners of the firms who wantedto run the Theatre without a valid licence in violation of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as the licence was granted to them only in their individual capacity and no licence in respect thereto had been issued in their favour. [955G H] 2 :3 The District Collector passed the order dated September, 26,1980. It was not one suspended the licence which was granted in his personal capacity but only as a representatives of the partnership. [975A B] 2(a) The impugned orders were not one suspend the licence and hence it necessarily follows that where the licensed premises including the cinematograph used therein belongs to a partnership and one of the members obtains a licence, the other partners automatically acquire interests in the licenceand that the privilege granted by the licensing Authority "must necessarily follow the title in such building and the cinematograph.

The appellants, who were displaced persons, entered into an agreement with them of a composite character consisting of three distinct matters. The appellant was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute related to a time before the merger of Dholpur. The Ruler of Jodhpur had granted a permit on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export further as his permit was not extended. On January 26, 1950, the State refused to refund the amount, but the suit was filed out of which appeal No. 20,855/ along with interest and costs. The appellant contended that there had been no recognition of the concessions by the new sovereign and reliance was placed on the continuance of laws in the covenanting States. Held, that article VI could not be availed of by the subjects of the new State as it stood before the Constitution came into force. The right to claim refund was taken away by any law competently passed. The rights of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the old States would notwithstanding the Covenant not be assumed by the existing State. The agreement did not create a legal right in favour of the appellant as it had been recognised by the old sovereign. The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights of subjects and undertook the liability if any of the erstwhile States. The present case was not one of recognition of an agreement but of recognition. The question whether the right to refund was given away by a law competent lawfully passed, could not arise in the present case because there was no recognition by the Ruler of the Rajasthan as it emerged on January 26 and 1950.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the conviction should be maintained but was not of opinion that the sentence in each case should be commuted to imprisonment; (2) the sentence should not be imposed and of the other that the appellants were not guilty and so should be acquitted, HELD: (i) The conviction under section 149 is not of a general nature. It is true that the conviction can be based on circumstantial evidence but it is equally possible that the circumstances must be such as to exclude every hypothesis except one which could have been taken into consideration in determining whether the accused had committed the offence and if overlooked will result in miscarriage of justice. [72 D E] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the convictions should be upheld but it was not necessary for the High Court to examine the evidence. It was not open to the High court to examine any other evidence on record which could justify its conclusion. [73 F H] (iii) In the present case, there is no evidence of any prior meeting. The injuries shown in the inquest report and the postmortem report do not tally. The medical evidence shows that the injury caused was the one on the neck. It does not show that the other two struck any particular blow. [74 F G] (iv) There is no charge under section 34 and, as Lord Sumner points out in Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs King Emperor, A.I.R. , referred to.

The appellant Corporation had issued two cheques for Rs. 50,000 on 27th December, 1960 and for Rs., 50, 000 on 27rd December, 1961. The deceased had issued three cheques for the first premium and the cheque for Rs, 50,001 was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount 354 was received by the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of the proposal. The appellant Corporation filed a suit for recovery of the amount paid towards the insurance contract on the ground that there was no concluded contract and non acceptance of it amounted to acceptance of proposal and the allegation about the assurance given to the deceased as alleged in the plaint was not true nor the alleged assurance if any valid under law. The Trial Court held that there had been no concluded valid insurance contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the appellant Corporation was liable for the risk and as such the plaintiffs had no right to claim and there was nothing to show that there were no concluded contracts and non receipt of the premium amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of a proposal. On appeal, the High Court reversed the Judgment of the Trial Court and held that the other averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment of the first insurance premium would amount to acceptance were false. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there is no concluded concluded contract between them and therefore the suit was not maintainable. It was further contended that the High court had erred in holding that there could be no concluded agreement and non accepting the proposal form was not sufficient averment that the Divisional Manager was the only competent authority to accept the proposal and as a matter of fact he had never stated that he had taken a decision to accept it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court 's criticism with the assertion in the written statement that there has been acceptance of an proposal and that like 358 other contracts, the contract of insurance was complete by offer and acceptance. [359E] 1.2 In the instant case, there was a general statement that the proposal forms were sent from the office at Guntur to the Divisional Office at Masulipatam, and exhibit B 13 is the copy of the Standing order. The endorsement therein of the assistant Divisional Manager read as follows: "NOTES AND DECISION : may be accepted at O.R." WITH E.D.B.S.R. AND DECITIONISION : might be accepted as a prima facie acceptance must be communicated to the offeror. [358G H] 1:3 The mere receipt and retention of premiums until after the death of applicant does not give rise to a contract, though the circumstances may be such that approval could be inferred from retention of the premiums. Mere delay in giving an answer cannot be construed as an acceptance, as, prima facie, acceptance must have been communicated to offeror.[358G] 1 :4 The mere filing and non communication of acceptance of proposals by the Divisional Managers does not make any difference between the terms "underwriting and revivals" of policies in case of Life Insurance Corporation and stated that it was the Divisional Officer who was competent to accept. [360H; 358A] 1.:5 In the present case, the proposal for insurance was sent from office at Masuripatam to the Regional Office at Hyderabad.

The appellant Bank of India Ltd. was the proprietor of a firm and its partners were partners in the firm. The firm had been dissolved by an order dated April 12, 1968 granted an interim injunction restraining encashment of the letters of credit pending disposal of the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in holding that an order granting interim injunction "is a final order" within the meaning of article 134(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution; (ii) the order of the High court amounts to a judgment or 'a decree. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The expression "final order" it has been held by a long course of authorities, occurring in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, section 109 of the Code of Civil Procedure and article 133(1) of that Constitution means a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; if the rights and liabilities of the party in dispute remain to be tried, after the order, the order is not final. [707 B C] (2) The High Court was right in holding in the present case that an ex communication was made by the appellant Bank on April 12 1968, and it was not contended that the order granting the interim injunction was a final one within the ambit of article 133 (1)(c). [708 F G] (3) The order of this Court amounts to an 'final order ' within the expression " final" in article 134 (1).

The petitioners are manufacturers of processed fabric and manufactured by the processor. In respect of civil miscellaneous petition, the petitioners have filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the order dated 4th November, 1988 passed by the Excise Commissioner, contending that the assessable value of the grey cloth plus the value of job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, would include only the price or deemed price at Which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. The petitioners have also filed a counter affidavit in this regard. In view of the fact that the petitioners are manufacturer of processed fabrics and manufactured from the stage stage stage, they have not been included in the price list for the purpose of determining the assessable valuation. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 346 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another, the information is required relating to the prices at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabil ities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. [346E] 1.2 Rule 174 enjoins that whenever goods owned or manufactured by one of persons are manufactured in another, then the information must be the value at which they are sold by the information was required relating t o the price to which the goods were sold by them. The price at that rate would include both the price and deemed price. [347G] 1:3 Rule 174 casts a duty on the manufacturer of grey cloth or fabric plus the amount of duty paid on the processed fabrics, because those would be post manufacturing profits. It is necessary to include the processor "s profits" which are post manufacturing profit. [348H; 348A] 1 :4. The value at that price would include all the expenses and charges plus profit, but not any other subsequent profit or expenses.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti in 1963, long before the Amending Act came into force. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974. On April 1, 1975, he was confirmed in that post in course of time. On May 1, 1976, he filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion as a head clerk in any event. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The right to be consider for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to claim promotion but whether the Panchayat Samitis had the right to appoint him to the post of Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service. [782B] (2) The appointment of the appellant to the posts of a Head clerk was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Ordinance came into operation on June 13. 1973. [682C D] (3) The appellant was promoted by reason of section 14(4) of the Amending act of 1973. He was appointed lawfully to the Post of a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. For these reasons, the appellant could not have appointed the appellant as a Headmaster on an Ad hoc basis. [613B] In the instant case, the appointment of appellant to a post of a head Clerk was made by the Loharu Panchayat Samiti after June 1, 1973 and that was the post which the appellant had absorbed in Government Service. The appointment was made without the authority of law.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that Mahant Shivshanker Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath Chaubey, also referred to as Uma Shanker Yati. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati possessed no personal property. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Amauli properties were purchased by Mahant Shiv Shankar Yati and that the income derived from the funds of the Math was not liable to be taxed under section 10(1)(a) of the U.P. Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Amaul properties were acquired by Mahant Ram Shivshankar Yati in 1921 from 662 the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivpher Yati; (ii) the income received from the fund of the temple was not assessable to tax under section 2(a)(i) of that Act, and (iii) the expenditure incurred on the maintenance of the institution was not taxable under section 3 of the Act. HELD: (1) The Amauli property devolved on Uma Shankar Yatati as properties of the math and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. [635C] (2) The income derived by MahantShivshankarYati was held in high regard on account of his personal learning and attainments, and had a large number of chelas including many affluent persons from whom he received personal bhents or pranamis of large amounts of money. It is true that the expenditure was incurred for the maintenance and management of the religious institution and it appears beyond dispute that by virtue of this will the Amaiuli properties devolved on the Uma ShankarYati as property of the Mahant Shivphar Yati, and therefore, a claim for exemption from levy was not made. The burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim is upon the plaintiff to establish that the properties in respect of which he is asking for possession are properties to the possession of which the he is entitled in the right in which he sues. [735D] (3) The burden is upon him to establish, that the lands in question were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivshhankar Yatti as properties belonging to Math Saut and that Sadasiv Yatri was in fact a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saun. [758E F] (4) The expenditure incurred by Mahant SHIVshankar Yadav for the management of religious institution is not taxable.

The appellants, who were displaced persons from the village Raikot, filed a revision application before the Custodian General. The Additional Custodian dismissed the revision application on the ground that no land was available in the village and that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. On appeal by the appellants it was contended that the appellants were not entitled to allotment of suburban land and that therefore their allotment was rightly cancelled. Held, that the order of the Deputy Custodian General was correct in law and the High Court was right in holding that r. 17 of the 1954 Act was applicable to the case. The power of the Custodian under section 19 of the Act to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment existing in favour of a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. It is not necessary to ascertain whether the property vested in the Central Government, the Custodian was empowered to deal with it. Under section 10 of the , the Central government is empowered to take such measures as it considers necessary or expedient for the custody, management and disposal of the compensation pool. Section 19 of 1954 Act deals with a transfer of property to an allottee by way of final settlement of his claim to compensation and does not deal with the question of allotment on a quasi permanent basis. The Custodian is empowered under section 16(1) of the . to allot such property to any person or class of persons. It cannot be said that the Custodian has no function to perform with respect to evacuee property.

Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The view of the High court was correct. [489C] 2. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest of the person who was the party to the suit.[490D] 3. The expression 'interest in the subject matters of the suits and the interests is the Interest of the persons who are the parties to the proceedings. [490F] 4.
