The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the State Legislature had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that it was impermissible for the Government to reduce the age from 58 to 55; and that as a result of the increase in the age, of retirement from 58 years in 1976, a vested right had accrued to the petitioners, which could be taken away if at all only from future entrants to the Government service; that as the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age for superannuation from 55 years to 58, they were entitled to continue in service until they were worn out and have "one foot in the grave", and that, therefore, the decision was bad for an total nonapplication of mind. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government had issued instructions by a notification dated February 14, 1983 for payment of "anticipatory pension" at 3110th of the last pay drawn in all cases wherein the sanction of pension was delayed. On the other hand, a sense of frustration and stagnation cannot be allowed to generate in the minds of the junior members of the services and the younger sections of the society. Such a fixation of age would be unreasonable or arbitrary if it does not subserve any public interest. [811B C] 1.2 The Government has issued instructions for payment to the youths h Is no relevance on the point of fixing the age. It is difficult to hold that in reducing the age by increasing longesvity, the State Government or the Legislature acted arbitrarily or irrationally. [912C D] Moti Ram Deka vs y., General Manager, North Frontier Railway, ; , referred to. 1.3 The Government of Andhra Pradesh had issued directions for payment on account of "excessive retirement" at the normal practice, and retention in service beyond that age the exception. was not applicable to the case of the petitioners. [1012D] Motiram Deka & Ors.

The appellants manufactured certain goods in the State of Bihar with the aid of raw materials. The sales were effected by the appellants in the course of export outside India within the meaning of section 5(1) of the C.S.T. Act, 1956. The Sales Tax Officer held that the sales effected by them were not sales in the nature of sales and that they were not liable to tax under the provisions of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Sales Tax officer. In further appeals, the High Court decided the issue against the assessees as early as 25.11.1987. The appellants contended that the Sales tax authorities had no jurisdiction to levy sales tax on the sale effected by their dealers in the state of Bihar and that the provisions Of section 9(1)(b) were not applicable to them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The words "within the meaning Of sub section (I) of section 4" have to be given full meaning; in other words, the exemption under section 9 has to be restricted only to export sales falling within the scope of section5(1). [348A B] Goodyear case ; , followed. (ii) The language of section 9 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947, does not tax purchases even in cases where the manufactured goods are disposed of only by way of sale inside the State or outside the State in India. If, on the other hand, the goods were sent 363 to the port by the assessee subsequent to and independent of the sale made by him, then for the purpose of that trans port, the assessee would only be an agent of the purchaser and the movement of the goods in pursuance of the contract of sale entered into by the purchaser would be one in the process of export within the ambit of section 6(1), but not under section 5 (3) of C. S.T., Purchases of raw material in the States used in the manufacture of goods inside the state attract the tax under section 4. [348C D] Good Year case ; ; , referred to. (iii) The word "sale" in section 2(p) of Act, is not defined in the Act but has been interpreted by this Court in Goodyear 's case. It does not include a sale in the sense that it includes a transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of a contract of transfer of immovable property. [349G H] Good year case ; and Goodyear vs Goodyear, ; , distinguished. (iv) The expression "sale in the context of sub section(1 ) of section 2 of the Central Sales Tax is not relevant for our purposes and it has to turn to section 2 (p). It does only tax purchases either in the 'penultimate sales falling under section 6 or such other sale within the ' meaning of Section 5(3) but not otherwise under section 10. [347C D, F] GoodYear vs Good Year, ; ; and (v) The definition of "sale " in section 3(1A) of Central Sales tax Act, 1948, does indicate that it is a transfer which takes place in the ordinary course of business and is not a sale within section 5.

The sellers of the goods were the owners of the cotton in question. The sellers received the bills of lading and it was on presentation of these bills that they continued to be the owners thereof till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the sellers ' contention that the goods remained the sellers property till they crossed the Customs barrier and therefore no tax could be levied on them under section 10(b). The High Court dismissed the application under article 226. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants : (1) that the sellers were not entitled to the benefit of article 285(1) (b) because the goods remain the sellers' property till the time they crossed this frontier and therefore the sales were exempted from tax under article 286 (1)(a). HELD: (i) The time of the export is when the ship with the goods goes to a foreign country. [927 C] (ii) The goods go out of the territorial limits of India. Therefore, the time of export commences to run when the goods cross the customs barriers. [ 927 D E] (iii) The normal rule in FOB contracts is that it is the duty of the buyer to obtain the necessary export licence. It is equally undisputed that the persons to whom M/s. The sales Tax Officer as also the High Court of Bombay have held that the seller and their buyers agreed in these sales that the property will pass to the buyer even before shipment. In other cases it has been held by this Court that the time when the export commences should be interpreted as the time at which the goods goout of the territory of India, [928 F G] (iv) The ordinary rule in international contracts is not that it was the duty and responsibility of the seller to obtain a necessary export license. It has been further held by the Supreme Court that where the intention as declared has not been carried out purchase tax should be levied. [1029 C D] (v) In the United Motor '8 Case (1), the time during which the export was commenced is when goods cross it and so the sales are exempted from taxation under article 285 (1). [930 G H] (vi) The circumstances to which our attention has been drawn are that the buyers and their sellers agreed in this sales that they will pass on the shipment of the consignments. In the instant case, the sellers and their buyer agreed in the sale that the ship will pass at the territorial limit. Therefore the time for the export should be construed as the period when the customs frontier is crossed and that it must proceed on the basis that the buyer and the seller intended that the Goods shall be the buyer 's property at the point of time when they crossed it.

The respondent divorced the appellant and her child. The appellant filed a suit for maintenance against the respondent on three grounds, namely: (1) that she was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she had now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant; (2) in any other case from the date of expiry of the period, if any, for which maintenance has been actually paid by the husband to the woman; and (3) in a case where the wife was divorced by or had obtained a divorce from her husband and had not remarried. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was a divorce and therefore ineligible for maintenance. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and restored the order passed by the trial judge. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1 ) there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was that there must have been a settlement by consent decree in 1962 whereby the respondent had agreed to adjust her then mutual rights; (3 ) in any case from a date when the divorce was actually paid, a subsequent series of recurrent does is 81 contra indicated and the husband liberated. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right to ignore is an absolute right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962 they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual relations between the quondum husband and the quarantum wife and they lived together; (4 ) in such a fact situation is the neglected divorcee. Surely, Parliament, in keeping with article 15(3) and deliberate by design, made a special provision to help women in distress cast away by divorce. [81G H] 1.2 The husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His plea is his right to ignored. In the instant case, there was no specific plea, based upon the latter provision, set up anywhere in the courts below or urged before us. [82A B] 1:3 The husband had not examined herself to prove the fact that he has been giving allowance to the divorce wife. He has not produced himself to establish that he is giving allowances for the divorced woman. His claim is his rights to ignore. In such a situation, the husband cannot claim under section 127(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section 125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [83B] 1 :4 The husband having not examined itself to prove his right, the dissolution of the marriage makes no difference to this right under the current Code. [84C D] 2.1 In a case of divorce by mutual consent decree, the wife is entitled to the benefit of maintenance allowance and the dissolution does not create any new right in her favour under the present Code. The husband is entitled only to the benefits of maintenance allowances and the dissolved marriage makes nothing more than a mere right to claim under s.127(3). [85D] 2:2 In the present case, the respondent has not been examined himself as to whether he was giving allowance or not to the appellant. His contention is his Right to ignore the fact situation in which she entered into an agreement to adjust his then mutual right. Payment of illusory amounts by way of customary or Personal law requirement will be considered in the reduction of maintenance rate but cannot annihilate that rate unless it is a reasonable substitute.

The respondents leased out the properties under two lease deeds in favour of M/s. 2 (Item No.1 in Schedule A to the plaint) and the appellant landlord filed their objections to the applications. The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the High Court, and, therefore, could not be heard by us. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. [822B C].

The petitioners, who were registered as Export Houses under the Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March 1979 in para 174 of the said Policy, made provision for grant of Additional licences to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the Import and Export Policy. The said applications of the petitioners were rejected by the authorities on the view that petitioners had failed to diversify their export of "Other Products" during the year 1977 78. 460 of 1988 herein) was dismissed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court and the said petitioners filed an appeal before a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for the grant of Export House Certificates in theImport Policy for 1978 79, and that the authorities were directed to issue necessary Export Certificate for the year 1978 79 within three months. In the meantime, the petitioners filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the order of the Division Bench. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the petitioners had not failed to carry out their export obligation in terms of the import policy and that there is no basis for classifying such Export Houses into two different categories on the basis of the date of issuance of the Additional Licences or on the ground that such a classification has no connection whatsoever with the object sought to be achieved by the Import Policy 1978 79. The petitioners filed this appeal after obtaining special leave from this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the Import Trade Policy 197879, the emphasis was only on the f.o.b. value of exports without taking into account the net foreign exchange earnings for a much larger percentage. [247E] 1.2 The import policy is permissible for any import policy to provide an exception to the rule and to declare that an importer might import a canalised item directly. [249F] 1:3 In the instant case, the Additional licences issued to the petitioners have expired in the meanwhile. Therefore, the wrong was undone. That 247 was not the issue before this Court.[250B C] 1 :4 The Additional Licences issued to them had expired in that meantime and therefore the correct classification of Export Houses as well as grant of additional licences to export houses was the f .o.f.b.. value of the exports. [251F] 2.1 The petitioners have not been able to import the goods which can be so imported under the prevailing Import Policy. They are able to export the goods in terms Of the import Policy prevailing at the time of import. Therefore the wrong is undone.[250G H] 1.:4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it would depend on the terms of import policy prevailing at that time of importation. [250F] 3.1 There is a more realistic appraisal of actual benefit to country 's economy by the exports taking into consideration the net Foreign exchange earnings after deducting the value of imports and additional licences are issued on the same basis. The aforesaid examination of the provisions contained in the Import/ Export Policy 1978 80 and the Import Export Policy 1988 91 shows that while in the import & Export policy 1978 79 the emphasis is only on f.e.b, value of export without taking note of the net Indian exchange earnings during a larger percentage.[250F G] 3:2 The petitioners are entitled to avail the same and are able not to import them under the prevalent Import Policy 1988 81.

The appellant, a manufacturer of fusel oil manufactured by the appellant, was assessed to excise duty under the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. The appellant filed an appeal before the Collector against the said order. The Collector rejected the claim on the ground that in any event under the Act and the Rules, the duty of excise is payable by the manufacturer on the manufactured goods. In the appeals before this Court it was contended that in view of the provisions contained in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Central Excises and Salt Ac ture Act, 1985, the value of the drums should not be included in the assessable value of goods when the packing is supplied by a customer to a manufacturer on its own cost. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plain language of the statute does not permit of any further exceptions being read into the Act. [982G] 2.1 In order to appreciate the controversy in this case, it is necessary to refer to the relevant provisions. Explanation (i) to section 4 of the Act provides that every kind of container in which it can be said that the excisable goods are contained would be 'packing ' within the meaning of the Explanation. It is conceivable that the wholesale dealer who takes delivery might have its depot at a very short distance only from the factory gate or may have such transport arrangements available that damage or injury to the cigarettes could be avoided. [ 982A] 2:2 The plain words used in section4(4) (d)(ii) of Central Excises & Salt Act are not intended to permit of further exceptions, being read in the context of the scheme of the old section 4. [986B C] 3.1 There is evidence that 90% of the goods were supplied in tankers and not in containers had no relevance at all and the 10% represent ed the entire quantity of excisable goods delivered in packed condition. The cost of packing, whether incurred by the manufacturers or by the supplier, has to be necessarily statutorily included in assessable value if necessary, by addition to the sale price, except only where the packing was of durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. [987D] 3:2 In the instant case, the respondent therein manufactured cigarettes in their factories. For the purpose of measure of levy on goods so sold, the cost of pack, whether incur by the seller or by supplier has to he automatically included in its assessable value, if necessary. The packing is not of duisable nature and is returnable only to facilitate their transport in small quantities. [988E F] 3 :3 In the present case, there was evidence that 95% of goods were delivered in drums. For this purpose, the manufacturer or by a supplier has also to be automatically included. If this question is answered in the affirmative, then in respect of the said goods so sale, the costs of packing including post manufacturing expenses and post manufacturing profit by observing that the contention proceeded on the assumption that a conceptual value governed the assessment of the levy. [990G H] 4:4 The plain reading of the definition of "value" as contained in Section 4(1) (a) of Act does not warrant any further exception being read to the expression "value in section 3 of the , which is of dura tion nature and was returnable by the buyer to the assessee. [989H; 988A] 5:5 The plain meaning of Explanation to section 2(d)(1) of that Act is that every type of container contained in which the excisable article are contained shall be deemed to be 'Packing" within the definition clause.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Headclerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. The Principal of the training school issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, Venkataswamy, the canteen contractor as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. The appellant produced the currency notes. PW 6 conducted the test with reference to the fingers of the appellant and he also received the amount on 22.10.1975. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended for the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the 337 behest of the accused had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appeli lant was guilty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The presumption arising under section 114 of Evidence Act is not attracted on the proved facts. [321B] State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; , referred to. The petitioner was a retired officer of the respondent company. He retired from service on or about September 30, 1984. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement i.e. for a period of six months. The company informed the company that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company rules. Instead of availing of that opportunity, the petitioner on March 3, 1986 moved the High Court by way of a petition under article 226 of the Constitution and obtained ad interim stay of the proceedings before the Estate officer. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the view expressed by the Single Judge in Harkishan Lakhimal Gidwani and reiterated in Govind T. At the very threshold it was necessary to set out a few facts. It held that the words 'any such property ' in section 630(l)(b) relate to property specified in cl. (a) of the section, namely, in sections 538 and 545. The Court also held that there was no reason to give a twisted and laboured interpretation to the provisions of section 630 of the Act which its plain reading does not permit. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The words 'Any such property' in section 629(l) (b) are self contained and independent of cl. ' (b). In other words, the expression 'any property ' used in cl.(a) is self contained. [630C] 2.1 In construing a provision of an Act which provides for prosecution of an officer or employee of a company for wrongfully withholding the property of the company, it would be necessary to ascertain whether the provisions are so construed as to make it impossible to apply to all cases where there is no such provision in the Act. [062D] 2:2 The words "any such thing" in section 630(1) (a), therefore, must be interpreted to mean not only past officers and employees of a Company but also to past officers or employees of the Company. [20063H;603A] 3:3 In construing cl. It would be appropriate to take into account the provisions contained in section630(l). The words used are "any property" in cl., (a). The expression 'such property ' is selfcontained and independent. The word 'officer or employee ' used as a verb `or ' in cl, (b), therefore must be construed to mean only the present officers and employee of the companies but also includes past officers, employees and employees. [600B] 4:4 In construing the words "such property" occurring in section 642(l), it would not be possible to hold that the expression "any other such property" used in section 634(1)(b), is self explanatory or independent of el. (b); but the words used must be given their colour from the context in which they appear. [ 600C] 5:5 In construing an Act, it is necessary to find out whether there is any provision in a statute which provides that a person shall be liable for prosecution under section 630. The expression "such thing" occurring therein must be read as including all things which are reasonably capable of being used in the commission of the offence.

The appellant was the owner of a temple. He had movable property of the value of Rs. 1,000/ . After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 (No. XI of 1952) he filed an application under protest and without prejudice 520 to the claim made therein that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The Charity Commissioner then appealed under section 72(4) of the Act before the Charity Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there was no evidence of long user of this temple by the public as a matter of right. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Sansthan had movable properties of the amount received by it from the Government and (2) the trustees of the temple were not members of a family or a specified individual, and therefore, the institution was not public trust within the meaning of section 2(g) of Bombay Public Trust Act, 1951. HELD: (1)(a) The Sansthan had immovable property of its value and that it was not an endowment property. [501 D] (b) The temple was a private temple and not a private one. It is true that the temple was not one of the properties of a specified individuals but it was a public religious endowment. But where the beneficiaries are not members or of a particular individual, then the endowment can only be regarded as public, intended to benefit the general body of worshippers. [525 D] The Sanad refers to the entry in the village accounts. There is significant recital in the document itself warranting a contrary conclusion. From exhibit 35, the first Varaspatra of February 28, 1869, one gets a full picture of the working of the Sansthan and the consciousness of the devotees themselves as to the public character of the deity. [500 E] (c) The Sanads were not made in favour of individuals as such in order that the beneficiaries of the gifts will be only those individuals. [601 D F] (2)(a). The Sanaspatra was a document which was executed by the Maharaj who happens to be holding the Gadi at the relevant time. It was not disputed by the appellant, that there were four documents exhibit 40,37,39 and 38 dated September 10, 1929, respectively.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, called upon the respondents to show cause why a writ in the nature of a writ of habeas corpus should not be issued by this Court directing the Superintendent, House of Correction, Byculla, being the second respondent herein, to produce before this Court one Govindji Deoji Halai, the father of the petitioner, who is also a citizen and was also a resident of Bombay. The respondents did not appear in person on the appointed day but on the next day, the 17th June 1955, an Advocate acting on behalf of the assessee wrote a letter to the Additional Collector purporting to show that he had been released forthwith. On the 7th September 1955, a rule was issued by the Court on that petition subject to the question of its maintainability in view of the dismissal by the 113 892 High Court of Bombay under article 226 of the Constitution. The petitioner contended that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, which is not uniform has become discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Consti tution of India. Held, that section46(2), by incorporating the different State laws which are not uniform had become discriminatory such discrimination was permissible and did not offend the fundamental right guaranteed by article 14. The classification may be founded on different bases; namely, geographical, or according to objects or occupations or the like. It is well within its rights to devise its own machinery for the recovery of its own public demand and that no person belonging to one State can complain that the law of his State is more rigorous than that of the neighbouring state. The two together make up the full measure of the 901 burden and if it is permissible to vary the burden at one end it must be equally valid to vary it at the other for the same or similar reasons.

The appellant, a member of the Indian Armed Forces, was employed in the Indian Army. He was working as a clerk in the Defence Department. On June 25, 1960, he was served with a notice under section 9A of the . The appellant challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that it was not covered by the expression 'inclusive of one hour ' and therefore, the notice was invalid. The Tribunal accepted the entire case put forward on behalf of the Trustees and the Union appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) There is no provision in the which breaks up the hours of work by interposing a compulsory period of rest as is done by the latter part of section 55 of the , and it is not compelled to fix only one interval or to make the interval of one week. [954 F] (ii) The crew at the Alexandra Docks got a specified interval of two hours for rest and this makes up their 9 hours' work and one hour interval for rest in sub rule (1) (a) provides that the number of hours constituting a normal working day for an adult shall be 9. [854 E] (iii) The definition of 'inclusive ' is not exhaustive but only illustrative. It may or it may not be. There is clear antinomy between hours of duty and intervals of rest in subsection (1), and the phrase 'inclusive Of one hour only ' governs the normal working days and not the number thereof. [889 G H] (iv) The expression ' inclusive of one day ' in sub section (2) of section 14 applies to all employments only and they are shown in a Schedule appended to the Act. Therefore, an employer can take actual work on any day upto 9 hours in a 12 hour shift but he must pay a double rate for any hour or part of an hour of actual work in excess of 9 hours. [879 G] (v) The provisions of section 51 are not as clear as the corresponding provisions of the and they have led to long arguments before us.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and basement were separately let out, the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the provisions of U.P. High Court Act, 1947 will apply to the present case and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that in view of the language of Section 2 sub clause (2) of the new Rent Act, the provisions contained in U. P. High Courts Act, 1948 would not apply to such suits which were pending on the date of commencement of this Act and therefore the decree for ejectment could only pass. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The language of Sections 39 and 40 of the Act clearly indicate that for a newly constructed building the provisions Of this Act will not apply for 10 years and therefore it is clear that during the pendency of the litigation even of 10 years expired the restriction will not be attracted as the suit has been instituted within 10 years from such date of completion i.e. on the specified grounds as provided in Section 20. [164D] 1.2 The language used in sub section (2), therefore, clearly indicate the intention of the legislature that for the newly constructed buildings the provisions will not applicable for 10 year and therefore restriction as provided for in Section20 can not be invoked and it is thus clear that within 10 year as provided under clause (1) of Section 20 the period of 10 year would commence from 160 the date on which the first assessment was made. [165E F] 1:3 The language contained in sub clause(2) is a decision of a Bench of two Judges. It will be clear that for 10 to years expired, the restriction would not be applicable and it was therefore clear that after 10 years as provided by Section 2 restriction of the167 institution of suit as provided therein will not come into play. [166G H] 1 :4 The language in sub clauses (b) and (2)(a) of section 20 is a judgment on the Punjab Act where the question before this court was about the language used. If during the course of the proceedings 10 years have elapsed the tenant will be entitled to the benefit of the provisions under this Act Sub clause (3) of Sec. 20 will not therefore apply and it would be clear from that language that for 9 years as prescribed in Section 2 restrictions of the nature mentioned therein will apply. [167D E] 1.:5 The language is plain and unambiguous and does not mean that the provision should be construed so as to give effect to the intention. [168E F; 169A B] 1.(a) In the instant case, the suit was instituted within 20 years from the date when the first suit was filed and during the proceedings even of 11 years expired. The suit had been instituted after 10 year i. e. on 15th July 1972. Therefore it could not have been contended that the present revision petition or the appeal either to the High Court or the appellate authority arose out of suit which was pending on that date. [169F G] 1(b) In view of Section 39 of the U. Pradesh Act, 1950, the period for 10 1 year would be 10 years. The restriction as contemplated in Section 21 can not have any application to the facts of this case and it cannot be contended that even if it is held that the rights of parties have to be determined in respect of the date from which the suit is filed still because of the wording of Sections39 and 40, the appellant tenant will get protection under this law.

The appellant was a thika tenant under the respondent. The suit was contested by the third defendant who filed a written statement in September 1948 contending that he had sold his interest by a registered sale deed dated April 12, 1949 to one Subasini. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. On appeal, the Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was entitled to possession because of the existence of any of the grounds mentioned in section 3(5) and that he could not be regarded as a thikika tenant inter alia on the ground that he sold his interests by a unregistered sale deed. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the suit had been filed before the Act but was riot disposed of by that date, and (ii) the decree was not binding on the landlord because of section 4(5). HELD: (1) The legislature always proceeded on the basis that section 4 was prospective. [183 D] (2) The Legislature always proceeded to take on the footing that section 3 was prospective in operation so as to defeat vested rights, but such operation may be given by express enactment or by necessary implication from the language employed. [184 E F] (3) Section 4(1)(a) of the Act is a general principle of law that statutes are not to operate retrospectively so as not to defeat the vested rights. The legislature never proceeded on any other basis functioning then. It was always proceeded with on the assumption that section 5 was prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish existence of one of the ground specified in section 4 in order to succeed.

The petitioners were appointed as Bench Secretaries Grade I and Grade II respectively in the pay scale of Rs.400 750 and 10 posts in the scale of pay Rs.500 1,000. The Pay Commission recommended that ten posts of Bench Secretaries should be upgraded and placed in the Pay scale ofRs.500 2,000 for Section Officers. The petitioners challenged the validity of the recommendations made by the Pay Commission on the ground that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court quashed the part of the notification dated July 4, 1976 which created Bench Secretaries grade I and the nomenclature of posts of Judges Grade II and Grade III respectively. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that Bench Secretaries were not entitled to pay scale admissible to Section Officers because they had voluntarily accepted the employment on unequal terms, the State should not deny their basic rights of equal treatment. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly quashed a part of notification dated 7th July, 1976 creating Bench Secretaries grades I and II in the cadre of Bench Secretary Grade II. [293A] 1.2 In Randhir Singh, the petitioner was a driver constable in the Delhi Police Force under the Delhi Administration. He was appointed as a Bench Secretaries in the High Court on the basis of a recommendation made by Pay Commission. The pay scale recommended by the pay Commission is as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 Fifty two posts of Benches Secretaries Grade II & Grade I & Grade II will be of the same duties and responsibilities. The criterion of selection shall be merit with due regard to seniority. [294B C] 1:3 In order to determine whether Bench Secretaries are entitled to higher pay scale, it is necessary that the nature of duties and functions of each post should be such as to ensure equal work. It must be determined by expert bodies like Pay Commission, Pay Commission and the High Courts. The classification so made in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. [295D] 1 :4 In Randhir singh, the petitioners were a driver Constable in the Punjab Police Force. They had been bifurcated into two grades with different pay scales. But it certainly is a constitutional goal. It requires among others that every Hon 'ble Judge will have one Private Secretary in the Scale of Rs,500 1000 and ten posts in Grade I shall be of same dutiesand responsibilities. [296C D] Randhir Singh vs Union of India; , ; P.P. Sharma & Ors. vs State of Haryana, [1987] 4 SCC 634; Randhir Singh & Others vs Union Of India; ; P P. Sharma and Ors. etc. vs Union Territory of Chandigarh & Ors., ; ; ; P K. Jain & Anr. vs Delhi Administration & Ors.; , ; ; D. Bhagwan Dass & Ors.. vs State Of Haryana, ; ; Randhir Singh and Ors., [1987], 4 SCC 635; Article 39(d) of the constitution proclaims "equal pay for equal work" . The differentiation so made is violative of the right to equality guaranteed under Article 14. [297C D E] 1.:5 In RandhirSingh, the Petitioner was a Driver Constable in Delhi Police force under the Punjab Administration. In the former, the arbitrary differential treatment in the salary scale accorded to some professors was struck down. He had voluntarily accepting the employment at unequal terms. The case of the petitioner for being put in the revised scale of ` Rs.200 400 for Section Officer was that he was appointed in sanctioned posts or not. [298D E] Randhir singh vs Union Public Service Commission, ; , ; D Bhagwan Dass and Others vs Stateof Haryana, , ; and P.K. Jain etc. etc., vs Union, of India & Ors; , referred to.

The appellant Company, a company owned wholly by the Government of India and that respondent 1 was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The State Legislature enacted the Madhya Pradesh Nagariya Sthawar Sampatti Kar Adhiniyam, 1973 which came into force on February 27, 1976. Section 127A of the Municipalities Act, 1961 empowers a municipal council to impose, in the whole or any part of the municipality, "a tax payable by the owners of houses, buildings or lands situated within the limits of Municipality with reference to annual letting value of the house, building or land called property tax". The appellant Company paid the contribution for the year 1976 as agreed. That amount not having been paid as provided in the agreement, respondent 1 terminated the agreement by its letter dated February 4, 1977. Respondent 1 terminated it by its letters dated February 04, 1977 and February 4 1977. The appellant company challenged the validity of the aforesaid notices on various grounds including that no tax was leviable on its property since the Company was owned wholly exclusively by the State Government of the India and therefore respondent 1 had no right to levy the property taxes by reason thereof. The Writ Petitions were dismissed by the High Court following the judgment delivered in the Writ Petition filed by it. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The power conferred by section 127A is not an absolute one but a discretionary power and must be exercised within reasonable limits. [127B] (2) The legislative field covered by Entry 23, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution is not in any manner defeated by legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69(d) of the Act of 1973. It was held by this Court that the State Legislature had a separate entity and its income was not the income of the State government. The appellant was granted a lease for twenty years to the respondent. On July 18, 1955, the appellant applied to the Board of Revenue for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah to him. The Board of revenue refused to ratify the lease and terminated it under the powers delegated to it under section 20 of the Abolition Act. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition No. 47 of 1956 in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated December 27, 1955. The principal question canvassed before this Court was whether the termination of the appellant 's lease by the order of December 27 was bad as it did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 Of the Abolition act. Held: (i) that the right created after July 1, 1945, are only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position, the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction. The words " such right" in the third proviso refer to the rights created before July 1. It is true that under the second proviso the Government can terminate the lease at its option and unconditionally under proviso (iii) that can be done only if it is in (1) I.L.R. , , referred to in sub section (2). But, as the third Proviso does not govern the second provisos, the notification of December 26, 1955 cannot be said to have been issued by the Government under the third clause. The effect of this rule is that rights created after August 1, 1946 are only void at the time when the party came into power later declared its intention to abolish all zemindaries and intermediary interest in land. A person can claim compensation only if his right is terminated by the State under "the foregoing proviso". In other words, while under the first proviso the government can terminate a lease at their option and partially under proviso(iii) it cannot, in our view, change the meaning of section 20 which we gather on a true construction thereof. The final step in the argument is 560 that the person Whose rights are terminated under the fourth proviso which is the " foregoing proviso" referred to In sub section(2), must, therefore, be entitled to compensation under sub section 1) of section 21 of the Act. A notice, dated 13th March 1951, falls under the latter proviso and is valid.
